title: The New Mission
paragraphs: § To the Ends of the World

Dear Theophilus — in my first book I wrote down everything Jesus started doing and teaching, right up to the day he said goodbye to the apostles he had chosen through the Holy Spirit and was taken up to heaven. After he died, he showed up alive to them again and again, in all kinds of situations, over forty days. Face to face, he talked with them about the kingdom of God.

Over meals together, he gave them a firm order: don't leave Jerusalem under any circumstances — wait for what the Father promised, the promise you heard from me. John baptized people in water, but you are about to be baptized in the Holy Spirit. And it's happening soon.
When they were together for the last time, they asked him, "Master, is this the time? Are you going to restore the kingdom to Israel right now?"

He told them, "The timing isn't yours to know — that's the Father's business. What you will get is the Holy Spirit. When the Holy Spirit comes on you, you'll have what it takes to be my witnesses — in Jerusalem, all over Judea and Samaria, and all the way to the ends of the world."

Those were his last words. While they watched, he was lifted up and disappeared into a cloud. They just stood there, staring into the empty sky. Then suddenly two men in white robes appeared beside them. "You Galileans!" they said. "Why are you just standing here staring up at an empty sky? This same Jesus, taken up from you into heaven, will come back just as surely — and just as mysteriously — as he left."
§ Returning to Jerusalem

So they headed back to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives — just a little over half a mile away. They went up to the upper room where they had been meeting: Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James.
They were all in this together for good — united in prayer, the women included, plus Mary the mother of Jesus and his brothers.
§ Replacing Judas

During those days, Peter stood up in front of the group — about 120 people were gathered — and said, "Friends, the Scripture had to come true: the one where the Holy Spirit spoke through David about Judas, the man who guided the soldiers to arrest Jesus. And now it has. Judas was one of us; he had his own assigned place in this ministry."

"You all know what happened: he took that evil bribe money and bought a little farm. That's where he came to a terrible end — his belly burst open and his guts spilled out. Everybody in Jerusalem knows the story; they call that place Murder Meadow. It's exactly what the Psalms said: 'Let his farm become a haunted ruin, so no one can ever live there.' And later: 'Let someone else take over his position.'"

"So Judas has to be replaced. The replacement must come from the men who stuck with us the whole time — from when John baptized Jesus all the way to the day Jesus was taken up to heaven — someone who, like us, is designated as a witness to his resurrection."

They nominated two men: Joseph Barsabbas, nicknamed Justus, and Matthias. Then they prayed: "Lord, you know every one of us inside and out. Show us clearly which of these two you've chosen to take the place in this ministry and leadership that Judas threw away to go his own way." Then they drew straws — and Matthias won. He was counted in with the eleven apostles.

title: The Holy Spirit Drops In
paragraphs: § A Sound Like a Strong Wind

When the Feast of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. Out of nowhere came a sound like a strong wind at gale force — nobody could tell where it was coming from. It filled the entire building. Then, like wildfire, the Holy Spirit swept through the whole group, and they started speaking in all kinds of different languages, exactly as the Spirit gave them the words.

There were a lot of Jews staying in Jerusalem at the time — devout pilgrims from all over the world. When they heard the sound, they came running. Then, one by one, they heard their own mother tongues being spoken, and it blew their minds. They couldn't figure out what was happening and kept saying, "Wait — aren't these guys all Galileans? How are we hearing them speak our own languages? Parthians, Medes, and Elamites; visitors from Mesopotamia, Judea, and Cappadocia; Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia; Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; immigrants from Rome, both Jews and proselytes; even Cretans and Arabs — they're speaking our languages, telling about God's mighty works!"
Their heads were spinning — they couldn't make sense of any of it. They kept asking each other, totally confused: "What is going on here?"
Others just joked, "They're drunk on cheap wine."
§ Peter Speaks Up

That's when Peter stood up — backed by the other eleven — and spoke out, bold and urgent: "Fellow Jews, all of you visiting Jerusalem, listen carefully and get this story straight. These people aren't drunk, whatever some of you think. They haven't even had time to get drunk — it's only nine in the morning! This is what the prophet Joel said would happen: 'In the Last Days,' God says, 'I will pour out my Spirit on every kind of people: your sons will prophesy, and so will your daughters; your young men will see visions, your old men will dream dreams. When the time comes, I'll pour out my Spirit on those who serve me — men and women both — and they'll prophesy. I'll set wonders in the sky above and signs on the earth below — blood and fire and billowing smoke, the sun turning black and the moon blood-red — before the Day of the Lord arrives, the Day tremendous and marvelous. And whoever calls out to me, God, for help will be saved.'"

"Fellow Israelites, listen carefully to these words. Jesus the Nazarene was a man fully accredited by God to you — the miracles, wonders, and signs God did through him are common knowledge. This Jesus, following God's deliberate and well-thought-out plan, was betrayed by men who took the law into their own hands and handed over to you. And you nailed him to a cross and killed him. But God untied the ropes of death and raised him up — death was no match for him. David said it all: 'I saw God before me for all time. Nothing can shake me; he's right by my side. I'm glad from the inside out, ecstatic; I've pitched my tent in the land of hope. I know you'll never dump me in Hades; I'll never even smell the stench of death. You've got my feet on the life-path, with your face shining sun-joy all around.'"

"Dear friends, let me be completely frank with you. Our ancestor David is dead and buried — his tomb is right there in plain sight today. But David was also a prophet, and he knew God had solemnly sworn that one of his descendants would rule his kingdom. Seeing far into the future, he spoke about the resurrection of the Messiah — 'no trip to Hades, no stench of death.' This Jesus is the one God raised up, and every one of us here is a witness to it. Then, lifted up to the highest place at God's right hand, he received the promised Holy Spirit from the Father and poured out the Spirit he had just received. What you see and hear right now is that outpouring. David himself never ascended to heaven, but he did say: God said to my Master, 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool to rest your feet on.' So all Israel, know this for certain: there is no more room for doubt — God has made him both Master and Messiah, this Jesus whom you killed on a cross."
Cut to the heart, the listeners asked Peter and the other apostles, "Brothers! Brothers! What do we do now?"

Peter said, "Change your life. Turn to God and be baptized, each one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ, so your sins will be forgiven. Receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. This promise is for you and your children — and also for all who are far away, in fact for everyone our Master God invites."
He kept going like this for a long time, urging them again and again: "Get out while you can — get out of this sick and twisted generation!"
That day about three thousand took him at his word — they were baptized and signed up. They committed themselves to the apostles' teaching, to life together, to the shared meals, and to prayer.

Everyone around was in awe at all the wonders and signs being done through the apostles. All the believers lived in wonderful harmony, holding everything in common. They sold what they owned and pooled the money so that everyone's needs were met.

Every day they worshiped together in the Temple, then shared meals at home — every meal a celebration, exuberant and joyful — as they praised God. People in general liked what they saw. And every day their number kept growing, as God added those who were being saved.

title: A Healing That Stopped Everyone Cold
paragraphs: One afternoon around three, Peter and John were on their way into the Temple for prayer time. At the same moment, some people were carrying in a man who had never been able to walk — not once in his whole life. Every single day they set him down by the Temple gate called Beautiful so he could beg for coins from everyone heading inside. When he spotted Peter and John about to go in, he asked them for money. Peter — with John right beside him — locked eyes with the man and said, "Hey. Look at us." The man looked up, sure he was about to get something.

Peter said, "I don't have a single coin on me. But I'll give you what I've got: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth — walk!" Then he took the man's right hand and pulled him up. Instantly the man's feet and ankles went solid and strong. He jumped up and started walking.

The man went into the Temple with them, walking around, jumping for joy, and praising God out loud. Everyone there watched him walking and praising God, and then it clicked — this was the guy who used to sit and beg at the Beautiful Gate. They couldn't believe their eyes.
The man was over the moon and wouldn't let go of Peter and John. Meanwhile, a crowd came running to Solomon's Porch to see what was going on.
§ Turn to Face God

Peter saw the crowd gathering and spoke up: "Listen, Israel — why are you so shocked by this? And why are you staring at us like we pulled this off with our own power or goodness? It was the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — the God of our ancestors — who brought honor to his Son Jesus. This is the same Jesus Pilate said was innocent, and you said no to him anyway. You said no to the Holy One, the Righteous One, and picked a murderer to go free instead. You killed the very Source of Life — and then God raised him back from the dead. We saw it with our own eyes. It was faith in Jesus' name that got this man — the one whose condition you all know so well — back on his feet. Yes — faith, and nothing but faith, made this man completely whole, right in front of you."

"And listen, friends — I know you had no clue what you were really doing when Jesus was killed. Your leaders didn't either. But God had been saying through every prophet all along that his Messiah would suffer and die, and he took what you did and used it to make his plan happen."

"So now it's time to turn your life around! Face God so he can wipe your sins clean, pour out blessing after blessing to refresh you, and send you the Messiah he picked out for you — Jesus himself. Right now Jesus has to stay in heaven, out of sight, until the time comes for everything to be set right — exactly like God said through his holy prophets way back. Moses, for example, said: 'Your God will raise up a prophet just like me from among your own people. Listen to everything he tells you. Anyone who refuses to listen to that prophet will be cut off from the people.'"

"Every prophet from Samuel on said the same thing — they all pointed to these very days. These prophets, and the covenant God made with your ancestors, are your family story. Remember God's promise to Abraham: 'Through your offspring, every family on earth will be blessed.' And you're first in line for that blessing: God raised up his Son and sent him to bless you — as each one of you turns away from your wrongdoing."

title: Arrested but Unstoppable
paragraphs: § Nothing to Hide

While Peter and John were still talking to the crowd, the priests showed up with the chief of the Temple police and some Sadducees — and they were furious. These rookie apostles were teaching the people and announcing that, in Jesus, resurrection from the dead had actually happened. So they arrested Peter and John and locked them up overnight, since it was already late. But many who heard the message had already believed — roughly five thousand people!

The next day, Jerusalem's power players called a meeting: the rulers, the religious leaders, the scholars, plus Annas the Chief Priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander — basically everyone who was anyone. They put Peter and John in the middle of the room and grilled them: "Who put you in charge here? What gives you the right to do this?"

Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, let them have it: "Rulers and leaders of the people — if we're on trial today for helping a sick man, if you're investigating this healing, then I'll be totally upfront: we have nothing to hide. By the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth — the One you killed on a cross, the One God raised from the dead — by his name this man stands before you healthy and whole. Jesus is 'the stone you builders threw out, which has now become the cornerstone.' There is no other way to be saved; no other name has been or ever will be given to us by which we can be saved. Only this one."

They couldn't take their eyes off them — Peter and John standing there so confident, so sure of themselves! And it got even more fascinating when they realized these two were ordinary guys with no Scripture training or formal education. They recognized them as companions of Jesus — but with the healed man standing right in front of them, standing so straight, so completely healed — what could they possibly say against that?

So they sent Peter and John out of the room to figure out a plan. They huddled up: "What are we supposed to do with these men? By now the whole town knows a miracle happened, and that they're behind it. We can't deny that. But to keep it from spreading further, let's shut them down with threats so they won't dare use Jesus' name with anyone ever again."

They called the two back in and warned them never, ever to speak or teach in the name of Jesus again. But Peter and John fired right back: "You decide what's right in God's eyes — listening to you, or listening to God? As for us, there's no question: we cannot keep quiet about what we've seen and heard."

The religious leaders threatened them again, then let them go. They couldn't find a single charge that would stick — nothing that would keep them locked up. The people wouldn't have stood for it; everyone was praising God over what had happened. And the man who had been miraculously healed was over forty years old.
§ One Heart, One Mind

As soon as Peter and John were released, they went straight to their friends and reported everything the high priests and religious leaders had said. Hearing the report, they all lifted their voices together in a beautiful harmony of prayer: "Strong God, you made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them. By the Holy Spirit you spoke through your servant, our father David: 'Why the big noise, nations? Why the mean plots, peoples? Earth's leaders push for position, rulers meet for summit talks — the God-deniers, the Messiah-defiers!'"

"And that's exactly what happened — they really did meet: Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with nations and peoples, even Israel itself! They met right here in this city to plot against your holy Son Jesus, the One you made Messiah, carrying out the plans you set in motion long ago."

"And now they're at it again! Lord, take note of their threats, and give your servants fearless confidence to preach your message — as you stretch out your hand to heal, and do miracles and wonders in the name of your holy servant Jesus."
While they prayed, the building where they met shook. Every one of them was filled with the Holy Spirit and went on speaking God's Word with bold, fearless confidence.

The entire family of believers was united — one heart, one soul! They didn't treat their belongings as private property. Nobody said, "That's mine — hands off." Everything was shared. The apostles gave powerful testimony to the resurrection of the Master Jesus, and God's grace rested richly on them all.

And so it turned out that not a single person among them was needy. Those who owned fields or houses sold them, brought the money from the sale to the apostles, and offered it up. The apostles then distributed it to each person according to need.
There was Joseph — the apostles nicknamed him "Barnabas," meaning "Son of Encouragement" — a Levite from Cyprus. He sold a field he owned and laid the money at the apostles' feet.

title: The Ultimate Lie Detector Test
paragraphs: § Ananias and Sapphira

There was this guy Ananias, and his wife Sapphira was totally in on the plan with him. They sold a piece of land, then secretly pocketed part of the money for themselves. They brought the rest to the apostles and presented it like it was the whole thing.

Peter called him out: "Ananias, how did you let Satan talk you into lying to the Holy Spirit and skimming off the price of the field? Before you sold it, it was yours. After you sold it, the money was yours to do whatever you wanted with. So why pull a stunt like this? You didn't lie to people — you lied to God."

The moment Ananias heard that, he dropped dead. Everyone who heard the story was shaken to the core with the fear of God. The younger guys jumped right in, wrapped him up, carried him out, and buried him.
Less than three hours later, his wife walked in — she had no idea what had happened. Peter said to her, "Tell me, is this really the full price you got for the field?"
"Yes," she said, "that's the price."

Peter answered, "So the two of you actually schemed together against the Spirit of the Master? Listen — the men who just buried your husband are at the door right now, and you're next." The words were barely out of his mouth when she collapsed, dead. When the young men came back, they found her body, carried her out, and buried her next to her husband.
By now the whole church — actually everyone who heard about this — had a serious, healthy respect for God. Nobody was about to trifle with him.
§ They All Met Regularly

God was doing amazing signs through the apostles — wonderful things happening all over among the people. The believers kept meeting regularly, in incredible harmony, at Solomon's Porch in the Temple. People admired them a lot, but outsiders were nervous about actually joining. Meanwhile, those who trusted the Master kept getting added, left and right — men and women both.

It got so intense that people carried the sick out into the streets and laid them on stretchers and mats, hoping even Peter's shadow might fall on them as he walked by. Crowds poured in from the villages around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and the tormented. And every one of them was healed.
§ To Obey God Rather than Men

The Chief Priest and his crew — mostly Sadducees — were provoked beyond measure by all this, so they sprang into action: they arrested the apostles and threw them in the city jail. But that night an angel of God opened the jail doors and led them out. "Go stand in the Temple," he said, "and tell the people everything there is to say about this Life." They obeyed immediately — at daybreak they were in the Temple, teaching again.

Meanwhile the Chief Priest and his allies called together the High Council, Israel's senate, and sent officers to the jail to bring in the prisoners. But when the officers arrived, the jail was empty — no prisoners anywhere. They went back and reported, "We found the jail locked up tight, guards at every door — but when we went in, there wasn't a soul inside."
The Temple police chief and the high priests were baffled. "What is going on here?"

Just then someone burst in with the news: "The men you locked up are back in the Temple, teaching the people!" So the chief went with his officers and brought them in — gently, because they were scared the crowd might riot and turn on them.

They stood the apostles before the High Council, and the Chief Priest laid into them: "Didn't we strictly order you not to teach in Jesus' name? Yet you've filled all of Jerusalem with your teaching — and you're doing your best to pin this man's death on us."

Peter and the apostles answered, "We have to obey God, not men. The God of our ancestors raised up Jesus — the One you killed by hanging him on a cross. God lifted him up to the highest place at his side, as Prince and Savior, to give Israel the gift of a changed life and forgiven sins. We are witnesses to all of this — and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God gives to everyone who obeys him."

That made them furious — they wanted to kill the apostles on the spot. But then a council member stood up: Gamaliel, a Pharisee and a teacher of God's Law whom everybody respected. He had the apostles taken outside for a few minutes, then said, "Fellow Israelites, think carefully about what you're going to do to these men. Remember Theudas? Not long ago he made a splash, claimed to be somebody important, and gathered about four hundred followers. He was killed, his followers scattered, and the whole thing came to nothing. Then, around the time of the census, Judas the Galilean showed up and built a following. He fizzled out too, and his people scattered everywhere."

"So here's my advice: leave these men alone. Hands off! If this movement is just human, it'll collapse on its own. But if it's from God, there's nothing you can do to stop it — and you do not want to be found fighting God himself."

That convinced them. They called the apostles back in, had them whipped hard, warned them never to speak in Jesus' name again, and let them go. The apostles walked out of the High Council beaming — they had been honored with the honor of being dishonored for the Name. And they didn't slow down for a second: every day, in the Temple and in homes, they kept teaching and preaching that Jesus is the Christ.

title: The First Dream Team and Stephen's Stand
paragraphs: § The Word of God Prospered

Things were growing fast — new disciples were joining every day. But then some tension broke out. The Greek-speaking believers (called "Hellenists") felt their widows were getting skipped over when food was handed out each day, while the Hebrew-speaking widows got served first. It didn't feel fair.

So the Twelve gathered all the disciples together and said, "Look, it doesn't make sense for us to stop preaching and teaching God's Word just to manage food lines. Here's what we'll do: pick seven men from among you — guys everyone respects, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom — and we'll put them in charge of this. That frees us up to stick with what we're supposed to do: praying and preaching."

The whole congregation loved the idea. They picked Stephen — a man packed with faith and the Holy Spirit — plus Philip, Procorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a convert from Antioch. Then they presented these seven to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.
God's Word kept spreading. The number of disciples in Jerusalem shot up. And here's the wild part — a whole lot of priests started believing too.

Stephen was overflowing with God's grace and power, doing amazing things among the people — clear, undeniable signs that God was at work. But then some guys from the Synagogue of Freed Slaves — people from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia, and Asia — started arguing with him. They tried to out-debate him, but they couldn't keep up with his wisdom or the Spirit speaking through him.
So behind the scenes, they paid some men to lie about him: "We heard him trash-talking Moses and God."

That got everyone riled up — the people, the religious leaders, the scholars. They seized Stephen and hauled him in front of the High Council. Then they brought in their paid liars to testify: "This guy never shuts up about destroying this Holy Place and changing God's Law. We even heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth is going to tear down this Temple and throw out every custom Moses gave us."
Everyone on the High Council stared at Stephen — and they couldn't look away. His face was glowing like an angel's.

title: Stephen's Mic Drop
paragraphs: § Stephen, Full of the Holy Spirit
Then the Chief Priest said, "What do you have to say for yourself?"

Stephen answered, "Friends, fathers, brothers — hear me out. The glorious God appeared to our ancestor Abraham back when he was living in Mesopotamia, before he ever moved to Haran. God told him, 'Leave your country and your family behind, and go to the land I will show you.'"

"So Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. After his father died, God moved him to this very country where you're living now. But God didn't give him any of it — not even a tiny plot to stand on. He did promise, though, to give the land to Abraham and his descendants later, even though Abraham didn't have a single child yet. God also warned him: his descendants would live as foreigners in another country, enslaved and brutalized for four hundred years. 'But,' God said, 'I will step in and deal with those slave masters, and bring my people out so they can worship me right here.'"

"Then God made a covenant with Abraham and sealed it on Abraham's body through circumcision. When Isaac was born, Abraham circumcised him eight days later. Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of the twelve patriarchs — and each of them faithfully passed the covenant sign down."

"But those patriarchs got jealous and sold their brother Joseph as a slave to Egypt. God stuck with Joseph, though. He rescued him from every trouble and got him noticed by Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. Pharaoh was so impressed that he put Joseph in charge of the entire country — even his own household."

"Then a famine hit the whole region, from Egypt all the way to Canaan, and things got desperate. Our ancestors were starving with no food in sight. Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt and sent our fathers to check it out. They confirmed it and went back a second time to buy food. That's when Joseph told his brothers who he really was and introduced the whole Jacob family to Pharaoh. Then Joseph sent for his father Jacob and the rest of the family — seventy-five people in all. That's how the Jacob family ended up in Egypt."
"Jacob died there, and our ancestors after him. Their bodies were taken to Shechem and buried in the tomb Abraham had bought for a good price from the sons of Hamor."

"As the four hundred years were nearly up — the time God had promised Abraham for rescue — our people in Egypt had grown huge in number. But now Egypt had a king who had never even heard of Joseph. He crushed our people ruthlessly — he even forced us to abandon our newborn babies, leaving them out in the open to die a cruel death."

"Right in the middle of all that, Moses was born — a beautiful, beautiful baby. His family hid him at home for three months. When they couldn't hide him any longer, they put him outside — and Pharaoh's daughter found him immediately and raised him as her own son. Moses got the best education Egypt had to offer, and he grew up impressive both as a thinker and as an athlete."

"At forty, Moses got curious about how his fellow Hebrews were doing, so he went to see for himself. He caught an Egyptian beating one of them, so he stepped in and floored the Egyptian to avenge his oppressed brother. He figured his brothers would be thrilled he was on their side — that they'd see him as God's chosen deliverer. They didn't see it that way at all. The next day he saw two of them fighting and tried to break it up: 'Come on, shake hands. Friends, you're brothers — why are you beating each other up?'"

"The one who'd started the fight shot back, 'Who made you our boss? Are you going to kill me like you killed that Egyptian yesterday?' When Moses heard that, he knew the word was out — so he ran for his life and lived as an exile in Midian. During those exile years, he had two sons."

"Forty years later, out in the wilderness near Mount Sinai, an angel appeared to him looking like flames in a burning bush. Moses couldn't believe his eyes, so he went closer to check it out. Then he heard God's voice: 'I am the God of your fathers — the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.' Moses was terrified out of his mind; he shut his eyes and turned away."

"God said, 'Kneel and pray. You're standing on holy ground — a holy place. I've seen how my people are suffering in Egypt. I've heard their groans. I've come down to help them. So get ready — I'm sending you back to Egypt.'"

"This is the same Moses they had rejected earlier, saying, 'Who put you in charge of us?' This is the Moses God sent back as ruler and rescuer — using that angel blazing in the burning bush. He led them out of slavery. He did amazing things, setting up God-signs all over Egypt, at the Red Sea, and out in the desert for forty years. This is the Moses who told the people, 'God will raise up a prophet just like me from among your own people.' This is the Moses who stood between the angel speaking on Sinai and our ancestors gathered in the desert — he took the life-giving words God gave him and handed them to us. Words our ancestors wanted nothing to do with."

"They missed the good old days in Egypt and whined to Aaron, 'Make us gods we can see and follow! This Moses who dragged us out here into the middle of nowhere — who knows what happened to him!' So they made a calf idol, offered sacrifices to it, and threw themselves a party to celebrate their brand-new religion."

"God was not pleased — not at all. But he let them have it their way: go ahead, worship every shiny new god that comes along, and live with the consequences. The prophet Amos spelled out those consequences: 'Did you bring me animal and grain offerings during those forty years in the desert, Israel? Hardly. You were too busy building shrines to war gods and sex goddesses, worshiping them with everything you had. That's why I sent you into exile in Babylon.'"

"And through all of that, our ancestors carried a tent-shrine for worshiping the true God, built to the exact blueprint God gave Moses. They took it with them when they followed Joshua into the land God cleared of pagans, and they kept it all the way down to David's time. David asked God for a permanent place of worship — but it was Solomon who built it."

"But that doesn't mean the Most High God actually lives in a building made by human carpenters and masons. The prophet Isaiah nailed it: 'Heaven is my throne room; I rest my feet on the earth. So what kind of house are you going to build me?' says God. 'Some place where I can get away and relax? It's already built — and I built it myself.'"

"And you are just as stubborn! Your hearts are calloused, your ears are shut! You keep deliberately ignoring the Holy Spirit — you're exactly like your ancestors. Name one prophet they didn't treat this way. Your ancestors killed anyone who dared to announce the coming of the Just One. And you've carried on the family business — traitors and murderers, every one of you. You received God's Law hand-delivered by angels — gift-wrapped! — and you threw it away!"

At that, they lost it completely — a screaming mob of catcalls, whistles, and insults. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, barely noticed. His eyes were locked on God, whom he saw in all his glory, with Jesus standing at his side. He cried out, "Look! I see heaven wide open, and the Son of Man standing at God's side!"

Yelling and hissing, the mob drowned him out. Then, in a full stampede, they dragged him out of the city and started pelting him with rocks. The ringleaders took off their coats and left them with a young man named Saul to watch.

As the rocks rained down, Stephen prayed, "Master Jesus, receive my life." Then he dropped to his knees and prayed loud enough for everyone to hear, "Master, don't hold this sin against them." Those were his last words. Then he died. And Saul was right there, congratulating the killers.

title: The Magician and the Road Trip
paragraphs: § Simon the Wizard

Stephen's death set off a wave of brutal persecution against the church in Jerusalem. The believers scattered all through Judea and Samaria — all except the apostles. Good and brave men buried Stephen, giving him a solemn funeral. There weren't many dry eyes that day.

And Saul went wild, tearing the church apart — barging house after house after house, dragging men and women off to jail. Forced out of their home base, the followers of Jesus became missionaries everywhere. Wherever they were scattered, they preached the Message about Jesus. Philip went down to a Samaritan city and proclaimed the Message of the Messiah. When the people heard what he said and saw the miracles — clear signs of God at work — they hung on his every word. Many who could neither stand nor walk were healed that day. Evil spirits screamed in protest as they were driven out. And the whole city was filled with joy!

Before Philip arrived, a man named Simon had been practicing magic in the city, acting like some famous VIP and dazzling all the Samaritans with his tricks. He had everyone, from little kids to old men, eating out of his hand. They all thought he had supernatural powers and called him 'the Great Wizard.' He'd been around a long time, and pretty much everyone was in awe of him.

But when Philip showed up announcing the news of God's kingdom and proclaiming the name of Jesus Christ, they forgot all about Simon. People were getting baptized left and right, becoming believers in droves! Even Simon himself believed and was baptized. From that moment on, he stuck to Philip like glue — so fascinated by all the God-signs and miracles that he wouldn't leave Philip's side.

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted God's Message, they sent Peter and John down to pray for them to receive the Holy Spirit. Up to that point, the new believers had only been baptized in the name of the Master Jesus — the Holy Spirit hadn't fallen on them yet. Then the apostles laid their hands on them, and they did receive the Holy Spirit.

When Simon saw that the apostles could give people the Spirit just by laying hands on them, he pulled out his money, all excited, and said, "Sell me your secret! Show me how you did that! How much do you want? Name your price!"

Peter said, "To heck with you and your money! Do you really think you can buy God's gift? That's unthinkable. You will never be part of what God is doing by making deals and offering bribes. Change your ways — right now! Ask the Master to forgive you for trying to use God to make money. I can tell this is an old habit of yours — you reek of money-lust."
"Oh!" said Simon. "Please pray for me! Pray to the Master that nothing like that will ever happen to me!"
And with that, the apostles headed out — still witnessing and spreading the Message of God's salvation, preaching in every Samaritan town they passed on their way back to Jerusalem.
§ The Ethiopian Eunuch

Later, God's angel spoke to Philip: "At noon today, I want you to walk over to that deserted road that goes from Jerusalem down to Gaza." He got up and went. On the road he met an Ethiopian eunuch traveling back home. The eunuch had been on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and was returning to Ethiopia, where he served as the minister in charge of all the finances of Candace, the queen of the Ethiopians. He was riding in a chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit told Philip, "Go catch up with that chariot." Philip ran alongside, and when he heard the eunuch reading Isaiah, he asked, "Do you understand what you're reading?"

He replied, "How could I, with no one to guide me?" and invited Philip to climb up into the chariot beside him. The Scripture passage he was reading went like this: "Like a sheep led off to slaughter, like a lamb silent before its shearers — he never said a word. He was humiliated and denied justice. And who can count his descendants now that he has been taken from the earth?"
The eunuch said, "Tell me — who is the prophet talking about here: himself, or someone else?" Philip jumped at the chance. Starting from that very passage, he told him all about Jesus.

As they continued down the road, they came to a stream of water. The eunuch said, "Look — water! What's stopping me from getting baptized?" He ordered the chariot to stop. They both went down into the water, and Philip baptized him right there. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of God suddenly whisked Philip away — and that was the last the eunuch ever saw of him. But he didn't mind. He had found what he'd come for, and he went on down the road happier than he'd ever been.
Philip showed up in Azotus and kept heading north, preaching the Message in every village along the route until he arrived at Caesarea.

title: The Ultimate Transformation
paragraphs: § The Blinding of Saul

All this time, Saul was hunting down the Master's disciples like a man on a mission — his mission was to wipe them out. He went to the Chief Priest and got arrest warrants for the meeting places in Damascus: if he found anyone there following the Way, man or woman, he would arrest them and haul them back to Jerusalem.
He headed out. Just outside Damascus, a blinding flash of light exploded around him and knocked him to the ground. Then he heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why are you trying to destroy me?"
"Who are you, Master?" Saul asked. "I am Jesus — the One you're hunting down. Get up and go into the city. Once you're there, you'll be told exactly what to do."

His traveling buddies froze in shock — they heard the voice, but they couldn't see a single person. And Saul, getting up off the ground, discovered he couldn't see a thing. They had to take him by the hand and lead him into Damascus. For three days he stayed blind. He didn't eat. He didn't drink.
Over in Damascus, there was a disciple named Ananias. The Master spoke to him in a vision: "Ananias." "Yes, Master?" he answered.

"Get up and head over to Straight Avenue. At the house of Judas, ask for a guy from Tarsus named Saul. He's there praying. He just had a dream where he saw a man named Ananias walk in, lay hands on him, and give him his sight back."

Ananias pushed back: "Master, you can't be serious. Everyone's talking about this guy and the awful things he's done — the reign of terror he's run against your people in Jerusalem! And now he's here with official papers from the Chief Priest giving him the green light to do the same to us."

But the Master said, "Don't argue with me. Go! I chose him personally to represent me to non-Jews and kings and Jews alike. And I'm about to show him what he's signed up for — the hard suffering that comes with this job."

So Ananias went, found the house, and placed his hands on blind Saul. "Brother Saul," he said, "the Master sent me — the same Jesus you met on the road here. He sent me so you could see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit." Before he even finished talking, something like scales fell off Saul's eyes — and he could see! He jumped to his feet, got baptized, and then sat down with everyone for a huge meal.
§ Plots Against Saul

Saul spent a few days hanging out with the Damascus disciples, but he didn't waste any time getting to work. He went straight to the meeting places and started preaching that this Jesus is the Son of God. People were totally thrown — they weren't sure they could trust him. They kept saying, "Hold on, isn't this the guy who tore through Jerusalem hunting believers? Didn't he come here to arrest us and drag us back to Jerusalem for sentencing by the high priests?"

But their doubts didn't slow Saul down one bit. He was on a roll now, and he went right at the opposition — debating the Damascus Jews into a corner and laying out the case that this Jesus is the Messiah.

After this went on for a good long while, some Jews started plotting to kill him — but Saul caught wind of it. They posted guards at the city gates around the clock, waiting to finish him off. So one night, the disciples pulled off a rescue mission and lowered him over the city wall in a basket.

Back in Jerusalem, Saul tried to join the disciples — but they were all terrified of him. Nobody trusted him at all. Then Barnabas stepped in and took him under his wing. He introduced Saul to the apostles and vouched for him, telling them how Saul had seen and talked with the Master on the Damascus road, and how in Damascus he'd risked his life boldly preaching in Jesus' name.

After that, he was in — one of them. He came and went freely in Jerusalem, preaching in the Master's name without holding anything back. But then he crossed paths with a group called the Hellenists. He'd been locked in a running argument with them, and they decided to have him killed. When his friends found out about the plot, they got him out of town fast — took him to Caesarea, then put him on a ship to Tarsus.

With that, things finally calmed down, and the church enjoyed smooth sailing for a while. All across the country — Judea, Samaria, Galilee — the church grew. The believers were filled with a deep reverence for God. The Holy Spirit was right there with them, making them strong. They thrived.
§ Tabitha

Peter set out on a road trip to visit all the churches. Along the way he came to Lydda and met with the believers there. He ran into a man named Aeneas who had been paralyzed in bed for eight years. Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!" And he did — he jumped right out of bed. Everyone in Lydda and Sharon saw him up and walking around, and it hit them: God is alive and at work among us.

Down the road in Joppa lived a disciple named Tabitha — which means "Gazelle" in our language. She was famous for doing good and helping people out. While Peter was in the area, she got sick and died. Her friends prepared her body for burial and laid it in a cool room.

Some of the disciples heard Peter was nearby in Lydda, so they sent two men to ask if he'd please come right over. Peter got up and went with them immediately. They led him to the room where Tabitha's body lay. Her old friends — mostly widows — were there mourning, showing Peter the clothes and pieces of clothing the Gazelle had made for them while she was alive. Peter asked all the widows to leave the room. Then he knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, "Tabitha, get up."
She opened her eyes, and the moment she saw Peter, she sat up. He took her by the hand and lifted her to her feet. Then he called the believers and the widows back in and showed them she was alive.
Word spread all over Joppa, and many people put their trust in the Master. Peter stayed in Joppa for a long time, staying as a guest at the home of Simon the Tanner.

title: No Favorites: Peter's Rooftop Wake-Up Call
paragraphs: § Peter's Vision

There was a man in Caesarea named Cornelius — a captain in the Italian Guard stationed there. He was a genuinely good guy. He'd gotten his whole household living in a way that honored God, he was always helping people in need, and prayer was his daily habit. One afternoon around three o'clock, he had a vision. An angel of God — as real as the neighbor next door — walked in and said, "Cornelius."

Cornelius stared, not sure he was seeing straight. Then he said, "What is it, sir?" The angel said, "Your prayers and the way you help people have gotten God's attention. Here's what I need you to do: send some men to Joppa and bring back Simon — the one everyone calls Peter. He's staying with Simon the Tanner, whose house is down by the sea."

The second the angel was gone, Cornelius called two of his household servants and one especially devoted soldier from the guard. He told them the whole story, every detail, and then sent them off to Joppa.

The next day, while the three travelers were getting close to town, Peter went up on the rooftop to pray. It was about noon. Peter was getting hungry and started thinking about lunch. While the food was being made, he slipped into a trance. He saw the sky open up. Something like a giant sheet, let down by ropes tied to its four corners, came down to the ground. On it were every kind of animal, reptile, and bird you can imagine. Then a voice said, "Go for it, Peter — kill and eat."
Peter said, "No way, Lord. I've never in my life tasted food that wasn't kosher."
The voice came back a second time: "If God says it's okay, it's okay."
This happened three times — and then the sheet was pulled back up into the sky.

Meanwhile Peter was sitting there confused, trying to make sense of it all, when Cornelius's men arrived at Simon's front door. They called out, asking if a Simon, also called Peter, was staying there. Peter was so deep in thought he didn't even hear them — so the Spirit nudged him: "Three men are at the door looking for you. Go down and go with them. Don't ask questions. I sent them."
Peter went down to the men and said, "I think I'm the guy you're looking for. What can I do for you?"

They said, "Captain Cornelius — a man who honors God, famous for being fair (ask any Jew around here) — was told by a holy angel to bring you to his house so he can hear what you have to say." Peter invited them in and treated them like guests.
§ God Plays No Favorites

The next morning he got up and went with them. Some of his friends from Joppa tagged along. A day later they walked into Caesarea. Cornelius had been expecting them and had his relatives and close friends gathered and waiting. The moment Peter walked through the door, Cornelius jumped up to meet him — and then dropped flat on his face, worshiping him! Peter pulled him back up and said, "Whoa, none of that — I'm just a man, no different from you."

They talked as they headed inside, where Cornelius introduced Peter to everyone who'd come. Peter said to them, "You probably know this is pretty unusual. Jews just don't do this — drop in and hang out with people from other nations. But God just showed me that no nation is better than any other. So when I got the call, I came — no questions asked. But now I'd like to know: why did you send for me?"

Cornelius said, "Four days ago, around this same time — mid-afternoon — I was at home praying. Suddenly a man was standing right in front of me, and the room was flooded with light. He said, 'Cornelius, your daily prayers and the way you help people have gotten God's attention. I want you to send to Joppa for Simon, the one they call Peter. He's staying with Simon the Tanner down by the sea.'"
"So I sent for you right away. And you were kind enough to come. Now we're all here in God's presence, ready to hear whatever God put on your heart to tell us."

Peter couldn't hold it in any longer: "This is God's honest truth — it's never been clearer: God doesn't play favorites! It doesn't matter who you are or where you're from — if you want God and you're ready to do what he says, the door is wide open. The message he sent to Israel — that through Jesus Christ, everything is being put back together — well, he's doing that everywhere, for everyone."

"You know what happened in Judea. It started in Galilee, after John preached that people needed a total life-change. Then Jesus showed up from Nazareth — anointed by God with the Holy Spirit, ready to go. He traveled around doing good and healing everyone who was beaten down by the Devil. He could do all of it because God was with him."

"And we saw it — all of it. Everything he did throughout Judea and in Jerusalem, where they killed him and hung him on a cross. But three days later, God raised him up, alive, where people could see him. Not everyone saw him — he wasn't put on public display. God had handpicked the witnesses ahead of time — us! We were the ones eating and drinking with him after he came back from the dead. He told us to announce this publicly, to be his sworn witnesses that he is the One God appointed as Judge of the living and the dead. And we're not the only ones saying it. All the prophets back us up — that through him, people find forgiveness for their sins."

No sooner had Peter finished speaking than the Holy Spirit fell on everyone listening. The Jewish believers who'd come with Peter were stunned — they couldn't believe the gift of the Holy Spirit was being poured out on non-Jewish 'outsiders.' But there was no denying it: they heard them speaking in tongues and praising God.

Then Peter said, "Anyone here object to baptizing these friends with water? They've received the Holy Spirit just like we did." No one objected, so he had them baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked Peter to stay with them for a few days.

title: Peter Explains Himself in Jerusalem
paragraphs: § God Has Broken Through

Word got around fast — before long, the leaders and friends back in Jerusalem had heard the news: the non-Jewish "outsiders" were now "in." When Peter got back to Jerusalem, some of his old friends — the ones big on circumcision — confronted him: "What do you think you're doing, hanging out with those people? Eating food we're not supposed to eat and wrecking our reputation?"

So Peter started from the very beginning and walked them through it, step by step: "Not long ago I was in Joppa, praying. I fell into a trance and saw a vision: something like a huge blanket, let down by ropes tied to its four corners, came down out of heaven and landed on the ground right in front of me. Crawling around on that blanket were farm animals, wild animals, reptiles, birds — you name it. I was mesmerized. I took it all in."

"Then I heard a voice: 'Go for it, Peter — kill and eat.' I said, 'No way, Master. I've never in my life tasted food that wasn't kosher.' The voice came back: 'If God says it's okay, it's okay.' This happened three times — and then the blanket was pulled back up into the sky."

"Right then, three men showed up at the house where I was staying — sent from Caesarea to get me. The Spirit told me to go with them, no questions asked. So I went — me and six friends — to the man who'd sent for me. He told us how he'd seen an angel right there in his own house, as real as the neighbor next door, saying, 'Send to Joppa for Simon, the one they call Peter. He'll tell you something that will save your life — you and everyone you love.'"

"So I started talking. I hadn't even gotten six sentences out before the Holy Spirit fell on them — exactly like he did on us at the very beginning. That's when I remembered what Jesus said: 'John baptized with water; you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.' So tell me: if God gave them the exact same gift he gave us when we believed in the Master Jesus Christ — who was I to argue with God?"

When they heard the whole story laid out like that, they calmed down. And as it sank in, they started praising God. "It's really happening! God has broken through to the other nations — he's opened up Life to them too!"

Meanwhile, the believers who'd been scattered by the persecution after Stephen's death had traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch — but they were still only telling their fellow Jews. Then some men from Cyprus and Cyrene who'd come to Antioch started talking to Greeks too, giving them the message about the Master Jesus. God was pleased with what they were doing and put his stamp of approval on it — a whole lot of Greeks believed and turned to the Master.

When the church in Jerusalem heard about this, they sent Barnabas to Antioch to check things out. The moment he arrived, he could see God was all over it — behind it and in it. He jumped right in with them, cheering them on, urging them to stick with it for life. That was Barnabas — a good man, full of enthusiasm and confidence in how the Holy Spirit works. The community grew big and strong in the Master.

Then Barnabas headed to Tarsus to look for Saul. He found him and brought him back to Antioch. They stayed there a full year, meeting with the church and teaching tons of people. It was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.

Around that same time, some prophets came down to Antioch from Jerusalem. One of them, named Agabus, stood up one day and — prompted by the Spirit — warned that a brutal famine was about to hit the whole country. (It did eventually come, during the reign of Claudius.) So the disciples decided each of them would send whatever they could to help their fellow Christians in Judea. They sent Barnabas and Saul to deliver the collection to the leaders in Jerusalem.

title: The Great Escape and a King's Epic Fail
paragraphs: § Peter Under Heavy Guard

That's when King Herod decided to go after some of the church members. He murdered James, John's brother. When he saw how popular that made him with the Jewish leaders, he went further and arrested Peter too — right in the middle of Passover Week. He threw Peter in jail and assigned four squads of four soldiers each to guard him. Herod was planning to put him on public trial and execute him after Passover.
The whole time Peter was locked up under that heavy guard, the church prayed for him like crazy.

Then came the night before Herod was going to bring him out to kill him. Peter was chained to two soldiers, one on each side — and he was sleeping like a baby. There were guards posted at the door watching the cell. Herod wasn't taking any chances.

Suddenly an angel was standing next to him, and light flooded the cell. The angel poked Peter to wake him up: "Hurry!" The chains fell right off his wrists. The angel said, "Get dressed. Put your shoes on." Peter did. Then, "Grab your coat and follow me." Peter followed — but he didn't believe it was really happening. He thought he was dreaming.

They walked right past the first guard post, then the second, and came to the huge iron gate that led into the city. It swung open for them all by itself, and they stepped out onto the street — free. At the first intersection, the angel left him and went on his way. That's when it hit Peter: this was no dream. "I can't believe it — this is real! The Master sent his angel and rescued me from what Herod had planned, and from the public spectacle the Jewish crowd was hoping to see."

Still shaking his head in amazement, he headed to Mary's house — the Mary who was John Mark's mother. The place was packed with friends who were praying. When he knocked at the outer gate, a young servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. But the second she recognized his voice — Peter's voice! — she got so excited to run and tell everyone that she forgot to open the gate and left him standing outside in the street.

But nobody believed her. They brushed her off. "You're out of your mind," they said. She stuck to her story and insisted. They still wouldn't buy it: "It must be his angel." All this time, poor Peter was still out in the street, knocking away.

Finally they opened the gate and saw him — and lost it! Peter raised his hands to calm everyone down. He told them how the Master had gotten him out of prison, then said, "Go tell James and the other brothers what happened." Then he left and went somewhere else.

At daybreak the prison was in chaos. "Where's Peter? What happened to Peter?" When Herod ordered Peter brought out and the guards couldn't produce him or explain what happened, Herod had them executed: "Off with their heads!" Fed up with Judea, he left for Caesarea to cool off.
§ The Death of Herod

But things went from bad to worse for Herod. The people of Tyre and Sidon had gotten on his bad side. So they won over Blastus — King Herod's right-hand man — to speak up for them, and put together a delegation to make peace. Since they depended on Herod's country for their food supply, they couldn't let the standoff drag on. On the day of the meeting, Herod put on his royal robes, took his throne, and gave them a big fancy speech. The crowd played along and shouted their flattery: "This is the voice of a god!"
That was it. God had had enough of Herod's arrogance and sent an angel to strike him down — because Herod had given God zero credit. Down he went, and he died, rotten to the core, eaten by worms.
Meanwhile, God's Word kept spreading and growing like crazy.
Barnabas and Saul, after delivering the relief offering to the church in Jerusalem, headed back to Antioch. This time they brought John along — the one they called Mark.

title: Paul's First Mission Road Trip
paragraphs: § Barnabas, Saul, and the Know-It-All

The church in Antioch had some great prophet-preachers and teachers: Barnabas, Simon (nicknamed Niger), Lucius from Cyrene, Manaen (who'd grown up around Herod the ruler), and Saul. One day, while they were worshiping God — fasting too, as they waited for direction — the Holy Spirit spoke: "Set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work I've called them to do."
So they commissioned them. In that focused circle of fasting and prayer, they laid hands on Barnabas and Saul and sent them off.

Sent out by the Holy Spirit on their new mission, Barnabas and Saul went down to Seleucia and caught a ship to Cyprus. The first thing they did when they landed at Salamis was preach God's Word in the Jewish synagogues. They had John with them to help out.

They traveled the whole length of the island, and at Paphos they ran into a Jewish sorcerer who'd wormed his way into the confidence of the governor, Sergius Paulus — a smart man, not easily fooled by fakes. The sorcerer's name was Bar-Jesus, and he was crooked through and through.

The governor invited Barnabas and Saul in because he wanted to hear God's Word straight from them. But the sorcerer — Elymas is his name in plain Greek — kicked up a fuss, trying to keep the governor from believing. But Saul (also called Paul), full of the Holy Spirit, stared him down and said, "You fraud, you servant of the devil — you're up nights cooking up schemes to cheat people out of God. Well, now you've run into God himself, and your game is over. You're going blind — no sunlight for you for a good long while." Instantly a misty darkness fell over him, and he stumbled around begging people to take his hand and lead him.
When the governor saw what happened, he believed — fired up by what they were teaching about the Master.
§ Don't Take This Lightly
From Paphos, Paul and his companions set sail for Perga in Pamphylia. That's where John quit and headed back to Jerusalem. From Perga, the rest of them moved on to Antioch in Pisidia.

On the Sabbath they went to the synagogue and sat down. After the Scripture reading — the Law and the Prophets — the synagogue leaders said to them, "Friends, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak."

Paul stood up, paused, took a deep breath, and said, "Fellow Israelites, and all of you who honor God — listen. God chose our ancestors and made our people great while they were still nobodies down in Egypt. Then he led them out with mighty power. He put up with them for about forty years out in that desolate wilderness. Then he wiped out seven nations in Canaan and gave their land to our people — all of that took about 450 years."

"God gave them judges to lead them, right up to the time of Samuel the prophet. Then the people asked for a king, so God gave them Saul, son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin — and Saul ruled for forty years. Then God removed him and made David king, with this recommendation: 'I've found David, son of Jesse — a man after my own heart. He'll do whatever I tell him.'"

"From David's family line, God brought Israel a Savior — Jesus — exactly as he promised. But first, John got everyone ready for his arrival, preaching that they needed a total life-change. As John was wrapping up his work, he said, 'Do you think I'm the One? I'm not. But the One you've been waiting for all these years is right around the corner, about to show up — and I'm about to step off the stage.'"

"Brothers and sisters, children of Abraham, and all of you who honor God — this message of salvation has been sent straight to you. The people and rulers in Jerusalem didn't recognize who Jesus was, and they condemned him to death. They couldn't find any real charge against him, but they demanded Pilate execute him anyway. They did exactly what the prophets said would happen — without realizing they were following the prophets' script word for word, even though those same prophets are read in their synagogues every single Sabbath."

"After they'd done everything the prophets said would happen, they took him down from the cross and buried him. And then God raised him from the dead. There's no arguing with that — he showed up again and again, in lots of places, to the people who'd known him well during the Galilee years. And those same people are still telling everyone he's alive."

"And we're here today with good news: the promise God made to our ancestors has come true for us, their children! He raised Jesus — exactly like it says in the second Psalm: 'You are my Son! Today I celebrate you!' When God raised him from the dead, it was permanent — no going back to rot and decay. That's why Isaiah said, 'I will give you the holy, sure blessings promised to David.' And the psalmist prayed: 'You will never let your Holy One rot in the grave.'"

"David, of course, finished the work God gave him and has been in his grave — dust and ashes — for a long time now. But the One God raised up — no dust and ashes for him! I want you to know, dear friends, that it's because of this risen Jesus that forgiveness of your sins can be announced to you. Through him, everyone who believes gets everything the Law of Moses could never deliver. Everyone who trusts in this risen Jesus is declared right and whole before God."

"So don't shrug this off. You don't want the prophet's warning to be about you: 'Look, you cynics — look hard and watch your world fall apart. I'm doing something right in front of your eyes that you won't believe, even though it's staring you in the face.'"

When the service ended, Paul and Barnabas were invited to come back and speak again the next Sabbath. As people headed out, a lot of Jews and converts to Judaism stuck with Paul and Barnabas, who talked with them at length, urging them to keep living in God's grace.

The next Sabbath, practically the whole town showed up to hear God's Word. But some of the Jewish leaders, seeing the crowds, burned with jealousy. They argued against everything Paul said and made an ugly scene.

But Paul and Barnabas stood their ground. "God's Word had to be spoken to you Jews first," they said. "But since you want nothing to do with it — you've made it crystal clear you have no appetite for eternal life — the door is now open to the non-Jews. And we're walking through it, following God's orders, doing what he commanded: 'I've made you a light for all nations. You will bring salvation to the ends of the earth!'"

When the non-Jews heard this, they could hardly believe their luck. Everyone who was destined for real life put their trust in God — they honored God's Word by receiving that life. And the message of salvation spread like wildfire through the whole region.

But some of the Jews stirred up the most respected women and the leading men of the city, scaring them that their precious way of life was under threat. Alarmed, they turned against Paul and Barnabas and ran them out of town. Paul and Barnabas just shrugged and moved on to the next town, Iconium — filled with joy and the Holy Spirit, two happy disciples.

title: Road Trip, Riots, and Getting Mistaken for Gods
paragraphs: When they reached Iconium, they did what they always did — went to the Jewish synagogue and shared their message. The message convinced Jews and non-Jews alike, and not just a handful. But the Jews who refused to believe started a whisper campaign against Paul and Barnabas, planting mistrust and suspicion in people's minds. The two apostles stayed a long time anyway, speaking boldly and openly, laying out the clear evidence of God's grace — with God backing up their words through miracles and wonders.

But then the town split — some sided with the Jews, some with the apostles. One day Paul and Barnabas found out that both Jews and non-Jews, egged on by their leaders, were planning to beat them up. So they got out as fast as they could and headed for the next towns — Lystra, Derbe, and the whole Lyconia region. And once they got there, they were right back at it, spreading the message.
§ Gods or Men?

In Lystra there was a man who couldn't walk — crippled from the day he was born. He sat there listening to Paul speak, and Paul, looking him straight in the eye, could see he was ready — full of faith that God could work. So Paul said, loud enough for everyone to hear, "Stand up!" The man was on his feet in a flash — jumping up and walking around like he'd been doing it all his life.

When the crowd saw what Paul had done, they went crazy, shouting in their Lyconian language, "The gods have come down to us! These men are gods!" They called Barnabas "Zeus" and Paul "Hermes" (since Paul did most of the talking). The priest of the local Zeus temple organized a parade — bulls, banners, and a crowd lined up right at the gates, ready to offer sacrifices.

When Barnabas and Paul finally figured out what was happening, they rushed in to stop it. Waving their arms, they broke up the parade, shouting, "What are you doing?! We're not gods! We're just men, like you — and we're here to bring you good news, to convince you to ditch these empty god-superstitions and turn to the real thing: God himself, the living God. We don't make God; he makes us — and everything else: sky, earth, sea, and it all."

"In past generations, God let all the nations go their own way. But he never left them without evidence — he made a good creation, sent rain, and gave huge harvests. When your stomachs were full and your hearts were happy, that was proof of goodness beyond anything you did yourselves." They talked fast and hard like that, and just barely stopped the crowd from going through with the sacrifice that would have honored them as gods.

Then some Jews from Antioch and Iconium caught up with them and turned the fickle crowd against Paul and Barnabas. They stoned Paul until he was unconscious, dragged him out of town, and left him for dead. But as the disciples gathered around him, he came to and stood up. He walked back into town — and the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.
§ Plenty of Hard Times

After preaching the message in Derbe and building a solid core of disciples, they backtracked through Lystra, then Iconium, then Antioch — toughening up the disciples, urging them to hold on to what they'd started believing and not give up. They were straight with them: it wouldn't be easy. "Anyone signing up for God's kingdom has to go through plenty of hard times."

Paul and Barnabas handpicked leaders for each church. After praying — fasting to focus their prayers — they committed these new leaders to the Master they'd entrusted their lives to. Then they worked their way back through Pisidia, came to Pamphylia, and preached in Perga. Finally they reached Attalia and caught a ship back to Antioch, where it had all begun — sent out by God's grace, and now brought safely home by God's grace. A job well done.

When they arrived, they gathered the church and reported on the trip, describing in detail how God had used them to fling the door of faith wide open so people from every nation could stream in. Then they settled in for a nice long visit with the disciples.

title: The Ultimate Showdown: Rules vs. Grace
paragraphs: § To Let Outsiders Inside

It wasn't long before some Jewish believers showed up from Judea insisting everyone had to be circumcised: "If you're not circumcised the way Moses taught, you can't be saved." Paul and Barnabas were on their feet in an instant, pushing back hard. The church decided to settle it by sending Paul, Barnabas, and a few others to take the question to the apostles and leaders in Jerusalem.

Once they were sent off and on the road, they told everyone they met along the way through Phoenicia and Samaria about the breakthrough to the non-Jewish outsiders. Everyone who heard it cheered — it was amazing news!

When they arrived in Jerusalem, the whole church — apostles and leaders included — welcomed Paul and Barnabas warmly. They reported on their recent trip and how God had used them to open the door for outsiders. Then some believers from the Pharisee group stood up to have their say. They'd become believers, but they still clung to the Pharisees' hard-line party stance. "The non-Jewish converts have to be circumcised," they said. "They must be told to keep the Law of Moses."

The apostles and leaders called a special meeting to talk it through. The debate went back and forth, getting hotter and hotter. Then Peter stood up: "Friends, you know perfectly well that early on, God made it clear he wanted the non-Jews to hear this good news straight from me — firsthand, not secondhand. And God, who sees right through any pretending and always knows what's in a person's heart, gave them the Holy Spirit exactly like he gave him to us. He treated the outsiders just like he treated us — starting at the very core of who they are and working outward, cleaning up their lives as they trusted him."

"So why are you trying to outdo God now, piling rules on these new believers — rules that crushed our ancestors and crushed us too? Don't we believe we're saved because the Master Jesus — incredibly, out of pure generosity — stepped in to save us, just like he did for people outside our nation? So what are we even arguing about?"

Dead silence. Nobody said a word. In the quiet, Barnabas and Paul calmly reported the miracles and wonders God had done among the other nations through them. The silence got even deeper — you could hear a pin drop.

James broke the silence. "Friends, listen. Simeon just told us how God, right from the start, made sure the outsiders were included. That lines up perfectly with what the prophets said: 'After this, I'm coming back; I'll rebuild David's fallen house; I'll put the pieces back together; I'll make it like new. Then the outsiders who are seeking will find — they'll have a place to belong — all the nations included in what I'm doing.' God said it, and now he's doing it. This was never a last-minute idea; he's always known he'd do this."

"So here's my decision: we're not going to weigh down non-Jewish people who turn to the Master with unnecessary rules. We'll write them a letter saying: 'Stay away from anything connected with idols, keep sex and marriage pure, and don't eat food that would offend Jewish Christians — blood, for example.' This is basic wisdom from Moses, taught and honored for centuries in city after city, every Sabbath."

Everyone agreed — apostles, leaders, the whole church. They chose Judas (nicknamed Barsabbas) and Silas — both highly respected in the church — and sent them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas, carrying this letter: "From the apostles and leaders, your friends, to our friends in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: Hello!"

"We heard that some people from our church came to you and said things that confused and upset you. Just so you know, they had zero authority from us — we never sent them. We've all agreed to choose representatives and send them to you along with our dear friends Barnabas and Paul. We picked men you can trust — Judas and Silas. They've stared death in the face again and again for our Master Jesus Christ. We're sending them to confirm face-to-face everything we've written here."

"It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to saddle you with any heavy burden — just these essentials: stay away from anything connected with idols; don't eat food that offends Jewish Christians (blood, for example); and keep sex and marriage pure. These guidelines are enough to keep things good between us. And may God be with you!"
§ Barnabas and Paul Go Their Separate Ways

So off they went to Antioch. When they arrived, they gathered the church and read the letter out loud. The people were hugely relieved and encouraged. Judas and Silas — both gifted preachers — strengthened their new friends with lots of words about courage and hope. Then it was time to head home. Their new friends sent them off with laughter and hugs all around, to report back to the ones who'd sent them.
Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and preaching God's Word. And they weren't the only ones — there were quite a few teachers and preachers in Antioch at the time.
A few days later Paul said to Barnabas, "Let's retrace our steps and visit our friends in every town where we preached God's Word, and see how they're getting along."

Barnabas wanted to bring John along — the John nicknamed Mark. But Paul refused; he wasn't about to take a quitter who'd bailed on them in Pamphylia the moment things got tough. They argued heatedly and ended up splitting up: Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus; Paul chose Silas and, prayed over by their friends and entrusted to the Master's grace, headed for Syria and Cilicia to strengthen those churches.

title: Singing in Chains: Earthquake at Midnight
paragraphs: § A Dream Gave Paul His Map

Paul traveled first to Derbe, then on to Lystra. There he met a disciple named Timothy — his mother was a devout Jew, his father Greek. The believers in Lystra and Iconium all spoke highly of him. Paul wanted Timothy on the team — but first he took him aside and circumcised him, so the local Jews wouldn't be put off. Everyone knew his father was Greek.

As they went from town to town, they passed along the simple guidelines the apostles and leaders in Jerusalem had agreed on. It helped a ton. Day by day, the churches grew stronger in faith and bigger in number.

They traveled through Phrygia and the Galatia region. They'd planned to head west into the Asia province — but the Holy Spirit blocked that route. So they went on to Mysia and tried to head north into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus wouldn't let them go there either. They pushed on through Mysia and came down to Troas, a seaport.

That night Paul had a dream: a Macedonian man stood on the far shore, calling across the sea, "Come over to Macedonia and help us!" That dream gave Paul his map. We got to work immediately, getting ready to cross over to Macedonia. Everything had fallen into place. We knew for sure now: God was calling us to preach the good news in Europe.

Sailing from Troas, we made a straight run to Samothrace. The next day we docked at Neapolis and walked from there to Philippi — the leading city of that part of Macedonia and, even more importantly, a Roman colony. We stayed there several days.

On the Sabbath, we went outside the city, down to the river, where we'd heard people gathered for prayer. We sat down with the women who'd assembled there and talked with them. One of them, Lydia, was from Thyatira — she sold expensive purple cloth, and she was known as a woman who honored God. As she listened intently to what was being said, the Master opened her heart to trust — and she believed!

After she was baptized, along with everyone in her household, she said with warm hospitality, "If you're convinced I'm truly with you in believing in the Master, come stay at my house as my guests." We hesitated — but she wouldn't take no for an answer.
§ Beaten Up and Thrown in Jail

One day, on our way to the prayer place, we ran into a slave girl. She was a fortune-teller, and her predictions made a lot of money for her owners. She started trailing Paul, shouting to get everyone's attention: "These men work for the Most High God! They're showing you the way to be saved!" She kept it up for days, until Paul — finally fed up — turned around and commanded the spirit inside her, "Out! In the name of Jesus Christ, get out of her!" And just like that, it was gone.

When her owners realized their money-making business had just gone bankrupt, they grabbed Paul and Silas — roughed them up and dragged them into the marketplace. The police arrested them and hauled them before the judges, accusing them: "These men are troublemakers — dangerous Jewish agitators undermining our Roman way of life." By then the crowd had turned into an angry mob baying for blood.

The judges sided with the mob — had Paul and Silas stripped and ordered them beaten in public. After beating them black and blue, they threw them in prison, telling the jailer to keep them under maximum guard — no chance of escape. He did exactly that: locked them in the innermost cell and clamped their feet in stocks.

Around midnight, Paul and Silas were praying and singing bold hymns to God. The other prisoners couldn't believe their ears. Then, out of nowhere — a massive earthquake! The prison shook to its foundations, every door flew open, every chain came loose.

Jolted awake, the jailer saw every door hanging open. Figuring all the prisoners had escaped, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself — he was as good as dead anyway — when Paul shouted, "Don't do it! We're all still here! Nobody ran away!"

The jailer grabbed a torch and rushed in. Shaking all over, he fell down in front of Paul and Silas. Then he led them out and asked, "Sirs, what do I have to do to be saved — to really live?" They said, "Put your whole trust in the Master Jesus. Then you'll live the way you were meant to live — and your whole household too!"

They went on to explain the whole story of the Master in detail — the entire family listened in. Nobody slept that night. The jailer took them in, cleaned up their wounds, and then — he couldn't even wait till morning — he was baptized, he and his whole family. Back at his house, he set out a festive meal. It was an unforgettable night: he and his entire family had put their trust in God, and the whole house was celebrating.
At daybreak, the judges sent officers with the order: "Release those men." The jailer passed the message to Paul: "The judges say you're free to go. Congratulations — go in peace!"

But Paul wouldn't move. He told the officers, "They beat us in public and threw us in prison — and we're Roman citizens! Now they want to quietly sweep us out of here with nobody watching? No way. If they want us gone, they can come here themselves and walk us out in broad daylight."

When the officers reported this, the judges freaked out. They'd had no idea Paul and Silas were Roman citizens. They rushed over, apologized in person, escorted them out of the prison, and then asked them — please — to leave the city. Walking out of the prison, Paul and Silas went straight to Lydia's house, saw their friends, encouraged them, and only then moved on.
