title: Riot in Thessalonica
paragraphs: § Thessalonica

They headed south through Amphipolis and Apollonia to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish community. As he always did in a new town, Paul went to their synagogue — and for three Sabbaths in a row, he taught them from the Scriptures. He unpacked the texts so they could finally understand what they'd been reading their whole lives: that the Messiah had to suffer, die, and rise from the dead — no other way — and that "this Jesus I'm telling you about is that Messiah."

Some of them were convinced and joined Paul and Silas — including a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few prominent women. But the hard-line Jews were furious about the converts. Wild with jealousy, they rounded up some street toughs and soon had an ugly mob rampaging through the city, hunting for Paul and Silas.

They stormed Jason's house, thinking Paul and Silas were hiding there. When they couldn't find them, they grabbed Jason and some other believers instead and dragged them before the city officials, shouting, "These people are turning the world upside down, and now they're here, attacking everything we stand for! And Jason welcomed them into his house — these traitors who say Jesus is king and Caesar is nobody!"
The city officials and the crowd were rattled by all this. They made Jason and the others post bail, then let them go while they looked into the charges.
§ Berea

That night, under cover of darkness, the believers got Paul and Silas out of town as quickly as possible. They sent them to Berea, where Paul and Silas again met with the Jewish community. The reception there was way better than in Thessalonica. The Jews welcomed Paul's message eagerly and met with him every day, checking the Scriptures to see if what he said held up. Many of them believed — including a good number of prominent Greek men and women.

But it wasn't long before the hard-line Jews in Thessalonica heard that Paul was preaching God's Word in Berea too. They wasted no time — they showed up and stirred up a mob scene there as well. With his friends' help, Paul slipped away — caught a boat and headed out to sea. Silas and Timothy stayed behind. The men who helped Paul escape took him all the way to Athens and left him there. Paul sent word back with them to Silas and Timothy: "Come as fast as you can!"
§ Athens
The longer Paul waited in Athens for Silas and Timothy, the more upset he got — idols everywhere! The city was stuffed with them.

He debated with the Jews and other God-fearing people in the synagogue. And every day he went out to the marketplace and talked with whoever happened to be there. Through these conversations he got to know some Epicurean and Stoic thinkers. Some of them sneered, "What's this chatterbox trying to say?" But others, hearing him talk about Jesus and the resurrection, were curious: "He's bringing in some foreign gods. Let's hear more."

They brought him to the Areopagus and asked for a public talk, where it was a bit quieter. They said, "This is new to us — we've never heard anything like it. Where did you get this? Explain it so we can understand." Downtown Athens was a gossip hub. There were always people hanging around — locals and visitors alike — waiting to hear the latest on just about anything.

So Paul stood up in the middle of the Areopagus and laid it out. "It's obvious you Athenians take religion seriously. When I got here the other day, I was struck by all the shrines I saw. Then I found one inscribed, 'To an unknown god.' I'm here to tell you about this God, so you can worship knowing exactly who you're dealing with."

"The God who made the world and everything in it — Lord of heaven and earth — doesn't live in handmade temples, and he doesn't need humans to run errands for him, as if he couldn't manage on his own. He makes us; we don't make him. Starting from one man, he created the entire human race and made the earth livable, with plenty of time and space — so we could seek God, not just fumble in the dark, but actually find him. He's not playing hide-and-seek. He's not far away; he's close. We live and move in him — we can't get away from him! One of your own poets put it well: 'We are his offspring.' Well, if we're his offspring, it doesn't make sense to think we could hire a sculptor to carve a god out of stone, does it?"

"God overlooked those times when people didn't know better — but that's over now. What's unknown is now known, and he's calling everyone to a radical turnaround. He's set a day when he'll judge the whole human race and set everything right. And he's already chosen the judge, proving it to everyone by raising him from the dead."

At the words "raised from the dead," the crowd split: some laughed at him and walked off cracking jokes; others said, "We want to hear more about this — let's do it again sometime." That was it for the day, and Paul left. But some were convinced right then and there and stuck with Paul — including Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, and a woman named Damaris.

title: Corinth: A New Team and a Nighttime Promise
paragraphs: § Corinth

After Athens, Paul went to Corinth. There he met Aquila — a Jew born in Pontus — and his wife Priscilla. They'd just arrived from Italy, part of the mass expulsion of Jews from Rome ordered by Claudius. Paul moved in with them, and they worked together making tents — that was their shared trade. But every Sabbath, Paul was at the synagogue, doing his best to convince both Jews and Greeks about Jesus.

When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul could devote all his time to preaching and teaching — throwing everything he had into persuading the Jews that Jesus really was God's Messiah. But no luck. All they did was argue and contradict him at every turn. Completely fed up, Paul finally washed his hands of them. "Fine, have it your way," he said. "You've made your choice; now live with it. From now on I'm spending my time with the other nations."

He walked out and went to the house of Titius Justus, a God-fearing man who lived right next door to the synagogue. But Paul's work among the Jews wasn't a total loss — Crispus, the synagogue leader, put his trust in the Master, and his whole family believed along with him.

As they listened to Paul, a great many Corinthians believed and were baptized. One night the Master spoke to Paul in a dream: "Keep going, and don't let anyone scare you or shut you up. No matter what happens, I'm with you, and no one will be able to harm you. You have no idea how many people I have on my side in this city." That was all Paul needed to stay. He remained another eighteen months, faithfully teaching God's Word to the Corinthians.

Then Gallio became governor of Achaia, and the Jews launched a campaign against Paul. They dragged him into court and charged him: "This man is convincing people to worship God in ways that break the law."

Just as Paul was about to speak in his own defense, Gallio cut in and said to the Jews, "If this were a real crime, I'd gladly hear your case. But this sounds like another Jewish squabble to me — one more of your endless nitpicky arguments about religion. Sort it out yourselves. I'm not wasting my time on this." And he threw them out of the courtroom.
Then the mob turned on Sosthenes, the new synagogue leader, and beat him up right in front of the court. Gallio didn't lift a finger. He couldn't have cared less.
§ Ephesus

Paul stayed a while longer in Corinth, but eventually it was time to say goodbye to his friends. He sailed for Syria, with Priscilla and Aquila. Before boarding the ship at Cenchrea, he had his head shaved as part of a vow he'd made.

They landed at Ephesus, where Priscilla and Aquila got off and stayed. Paul went ashore briefly to preach to the Jews in the synagogue. They wanted him to stay longer, but he couldn't. As he said goodbye, he promised, "I'll be back, God willing."
From Ephesus he sailed to Caesarea. He greeted the church there, then went on to Antioch, wrapping up the journey.

After spending a good while with the Christians in Antioch, Paul set out again through Galatia and Phrygia, retracing his old route — town after town, encouraging the disciples and giving them fresh heart.

A man named Apollos arrived in Ephesus. He was a Jew from Alexandria, Egypt — a brilliant speaker, eloquent and powerful when he preached the Scriptures. He knew the way of the Master well and was on fire with enthusiasm. Everything he taught about Jesus was accurate as far as it went — but he only knew up to John's baptism. He preached boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and filled in the rest of the story.

When Apollos decided to go on to Achaia, his friends in Ephesus blessed the plan and wrote a letter of introduction, urging the disciples there to welcome him warmly. It paid off: Apollos was a huge help to the believers there, who'd come to faith through God's incredible grace. He was especially effective debating the Jews in public, laying out proof after proof from the Scriptures that Jesus really was God's Messiah.

title: Power and Panic in Ephesus
paragraphs: While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul traveled down through the hill country and arrived at Ephesus, where he found some disciples. The first thing he asked them was, "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? Did you take God into your mind only, or did you embrace him with your heart too? Did he get inside you?" "We've never even heard of that — a Holy Spirit? God living inside us?"
"Then how were you baptized?" Paul asked. "In John's baptism," they said.

"That explains it," said Paul. "John preached a baptism of radical life-change, to get people ready for the One coming after him — who turned out to be Jesus. If you were baptized with John's baptism, you're ready now for the real thing: Jesus."

And they were ready. As soon as they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Master Jesus. Paul laid his hands on them, and the Holy Spirit came into them. From that moment on, they were praising God in tongues and speaking about what God was doing. There were about twelve of them altogether that day.

Paul went straight to the synagogue. For three months he had the run of the place, working hard to make the kingdom of God real and convincing to them. But then opposition started building, as some of them spread nasty rumors through the congregation about the Christian way of life. So Paul left, taking the disciples with him, and set up in the lecture hall of Tyrannus, teaching there every day. He kept this up for two years, giving everyone in the Asia province — Jews and Greeks alike — plenty of chance to hear the message about the Master.
§ Witches Came out of the Woodwork

God did extraordinary things through Paul — way out of the ordinary. Word spread, and people started taking pieces of cloth — handkerchiefs, aprons, things like that — that had touched Paul's skin, and laying them on the sick. The touch did it — they were healed and made whole.

Some traveling Jewish exorcists who happened to be in town tried to copy what they thought was Paul's "trick." They started invoking the name of the Master Jesus over people troubled by evil spirits, saying, "I command you by the Jesus that Paul preaches!" Seven sons of a man named Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were trying this on one man when the evil spirit answered back: "Jesus I know, and Paul I've heard of — but who are you?" Then the possessed man snapped — lunged at the exorcists, overpowered them all, and ripped their clothes off. Naked and bleeding, they ran for their lives.

The story spread fast all over Ephesus, among Jews and Greeks alike. Everyone realized God was behind all of this. Curiosity about Paul turned into deep respect for the Master Jesus. Many believers came out into the open and made a clean break with their secret magic practices. Sorcerers of every kind came out of the woodwork with their spell books and piled them into a massive bonfire. Someone figured the books were worth fifty thousand silver coins. It became obvious: the Word of the Master was taking over Ephesus.
§ The Goddess Artemis

After all this had peaked, Paul decided it was time to move on through Macedonia and Achaia, and from there to Jerusalem. "Then," he said, "I'm off to Rome. I've got to see Rome!" He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, ahead to Macedonia, while he stayed a while longer to wrap things up in Asia.

But before he could leave, a massive uproar broke out over what people were now calling "the Way." A silversmith named Demetrius ran a thriving business making silver shrines of the goddess Artemis, employing quite a few craftsmen. He gathered his workers and others in the same trade and said, "Men, you know we've got a good thing going here — and you've seen how Paul has barged in and trashed what we do, telling people that gods made by human hands aren't gods at all. Tons of people are buying into it, not just here in Ephesus but all across the Asia province."

"It's not just our business that's about to collapse — the temple of our great goddess Artemis is going to end up a pile of rubble as her glorious reputation fades to nothing. And this isn't just local — the whole world worships our Artemis!"

That set them off like crazy. They rushed into the streets shouting, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians! Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" They threw the whole city into chaos, stampeded into the theater, dragging along two of Paul's companions — Gaius and Aristarchus, both Macedonians. Paul wanted to go in after them, but the disciples wouldn't let him. Some prominent city officials who'd become friendly toward Paul sent the same message: "Whatever you do, don't go near that mob!"

People were shouting all different things. Most of them didn't even know why they were there. The Jews pushed Alexander forward, hoping he'd take charge, and different groups tried to get him on their side. He waved them off and calmed the crowd with a sweeping gesture. But the moment he opened his mouth and they realized he was a Jew, they drowned him out: "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians! Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" — over and over, for more than two hours.

Finally the city clerk quieted the mob and said, "Fellow citizens, does anyone anywhere not know that our great city of Ephesus guards the temple of the great Artemis and her sacred image that fell from heaven? Since nobody can argue with that, you'd better calm down. This behavior is beneath Artemis. These men you've dragged in here haven't done anything against our temple or our goddess."

"So if Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen have a complaint, the courts are open — they can file charges there. If there's anything else, it should be settled at a legal assembly. There's no excuse for what happened today. You're putting our city in serious danger — Rome does not look kindly on riots." With that, he dismissed the crowd.

title: Goodbye Tour: Paul Heads to Jerusalem
paragraphs: § Macedonia and Greece

With things back to normal, Paul gathered the disciples and encouraged them to keep up the good work in Ephesus. Then, after saying goodbye, he left for Macedonia. As he traveled through the region, going from one gathering to the next, he kept encouraging everyone — lifting their spirits and filling them with fresh hope.

Then he arrived in Greece and stayed three months. Just as he was about to sail for Syria, the Jews hatched a plot against him. So he changed plans — went back by land through Macedonia — and slipped away from them. His travel companions were Sopater, son of Pyrrhus, from Berea; Aristarchus and Secundus, both from Thessalonica; Gaius from Derbe; Timothy; and two from the Asia province, Tychicus and Trophimus.
They traveled ahead and waited for us at Troas. We stayed on in Philippi through Passover week, then sailed off. Five days later we rejoined them at Troas and spent a week there.

We met on Sunday to worship and share the Master's Supper. Paul spoke to the congregation. We'd planned to leave first thing in the morning, but Paul kept talking — way past midnight. We were meeting in a well-lit upstairs room. A young man named Eutychus was sitting in an open window. As Paul went on and on, Eutychus drifted off to sleep and fell out the third-story window. When they picked him up, he was dead.

Paul went down, threw himself on the boy, and hugged him tight. "Stop crying," he said. "He's alive!" Then Paul went back upstairs, shared the Master's Supper, and kept on telling stories of faith until dawn! Then they left — Paul one way, the congregation the other — leading the boy away alive, and full of life themselves.

Meanwhile, the rest of us had gone ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, where we were supposed to pick up Paul. Paul had wanted to walk there, so he'd arranged it that way earlier. Everything went as planned: we met him at Assos, took him aboard, and sailed to Mitylene. The next day we anchored off Chios, a day later off Samos, and then reached Miletus. Paul had decided to skip Ephesus so he wouldn't get held up in the Asia province. He was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem in time for Pentecost, if at all possible.
§ On to Jerusalem

From Miletus he sent word to Ephesus, asking the church leaders to come to him. When they arrived, he said, "You know that from the very first day I set foot in Asia, I was with you completely — risking my life, serving the Master no matter what, putting up with endless schemes from Jews who wanted to kill me. I never held back or watered down anything. Every truth and encouragement that could make a difference for you, you got. I taught you in public and I taught you in your homes, urging Jews and Greeks alike toward a radical turnaround before God and an equally radical trust in our Master Jesus."

"But now there's another urgency pulling me. I feel I have to go to Jerusalem. I have no idea what will happen when I get there. I do know it won't be easy — the Holy Spirit has told me clearly, over and over, that hard times and prison are ahead. But that hardly matters. What matters most to me is finishing what God started: the job the Master Jesus gave me — telling everyone I meet about this unbelievably generous grace of God."

"So this is goodbye. You're not going to see me again, and I won't see you — all of you I've spent so long with, proclaiming the news of God's kingdom. I've done my best for you, given you everything I had, held back nothing of what God wanted for you."

"Now it's up to you. Stay alert — for yourselves and for your flock. The Holy Spirit has put you in charge of these people — God's own people — to guard and protect them. God himself thought they were worth dying for."

"I know that as soon as I'm gone, vicious wolves will show up and tear into this flock — men from your own ranks twisting words to lure disciples into following them instead of Jesus. So stay awake and keep your guard up. Remember those three years I spent with you, never letting up, pouring my heart out with each one of you."
"Now I entrust you to God — our wonderful God, whose gracious Word can mold you into what he intends you to be and supply everything you could ever need among this family of holy friends."

"As you well know, I've never had any hunger for wealth or fancy things. With these hands I earned what I needed and provided for those who worked with me. In everything I've done, I've shown you how important it is to work hard for the weak and never exploit them. You won't go wrong if you keep remembering what our Master said: 'You're far happier giving than getting.'"

Then Paul knelt down — all of them kneeling with him — and prayed. And then came a flood of tears. Lots of hugging Paul, not wanting to let him go. They knew they'd never see him again — he'd told them plainly. The pain cut deep. Then, bravely, they walked him down to the ship.

title: Paul Against the World
paragraphs: § Tyre and Caesarea

And so, with the tearful goodbyes behind us, we were off. We sailed straight to Cos, reached Rhodes the next day, and then Patara. There we found a ship headed straight for Phoenicia, boarded it, and set sail. Cyprus appeared on our left but soon disappeared from view as we kept course for Syria, finally docking at Tyre. While the cargo was being unloaded, we looked up the local disciples and stayed with them seven days. Their message to Paul, from insight the Spirit gave them, was "Don't go to Jerusalem."

When our time was up, they walked us out of the city to the docks. Everyone came — men, women, children. They turned it into a farewell party! We all knelt together on the beach and prayed. Then, after one more round of goodbyes, we boarded the ship while they headed back home.

A short hop from Tyre to Ptolemais finished the voyage. We greeted our Christian friends there and stayed with them a day. In the morning we went on to Caesarea and stayed with Philip the Evangelist, one of "the Seven." Philip had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.

After we'd been visiting for several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea to see us. He walked straight up to Paul, took Paul's belt, and — in a dramatic gesture — tied his own hands and feet with it. He said, "This is what the Holy Spirit says: The Jews in Jerusalem are going to tie up the owner of this belt just like this and hand him over to the godless Gentiles."

When we heard that, we and everyone there begged Paul not to be stubborn about going to Jerusalem. But Paul wouldn't budge: "Why all this drama? Why are you making a scene and making this even harder for me? You've got it backwards. The issue in Jerusalem isn't what they do to me — arrest or even murder — but what the Master Jesus does through my obedience. Can't you see that?"
We could see we weren't changing his mind one bit, so we gave up. "It's in God's hands now," we said. "Master, you handle it."

Before long we had our bags packed and were on our way to Jerusalem. Some disciples from Caesarea came with us and took us to the home of Mnason, who welcomed us warmly as his guests. Mnason was from Cyprus and had been one of the earliest disciples.
§ Jerusalem

In Jerusalem, our friends were thrilled to see us and welcomed us with open arms. First thing the next morning, we took Paul to see James. All the church leaders were there. After greetings and small talk, Paul told the story, detail by detail, of what God had done among the non-Jewish peoples through his ministry. They listened with delight and gave God the glory.

They had a story to tell too: "Just look at what's been happening here — thousands upon thousands of God-fearing Jews have believed in Jesus! But there's a problem, because they're more passionate than ever about keeping the Law of Moses. They've been told that you advise Jewish believers living among non-Jewish outsiders to go easy on Moses — telling them they don't need to circumcise their children or keep the old traditions. That's not going over well at all."

"We're worried about what'll happen when they find out you're in town. There's bound to be trouble. So here's what we want you to do: There are four men in our group who've taken a vow involving ritual purification but can't afford the expenses. Join these men in their vow and cover their costs. Then everyone will see there's nothing to the rumors about you, and that you actually take the laws of Moses very seriously."

"In asking you to do this, we're not backing out of our agreement about non-Jewish believers. We still hold to what we wrote in that letter: stay away from anything connected with idols; avoid food that offends Jewish Christians; keep sex and marriage pure."

So Paul did it — took the men, joined them in their vow, and paid their expenses. The next day he went to the Temple to make it official and stayed there until the proper sacrifices had been offered for each of them.
§ Paul Under Arrest

When the seven days of purification were almost over, some Jews from the Ephesus area spotted him in the Temple. Immediately they threw the whole place into chaos. They grabbed Paul and started screaming at the top of their lungs, "Help! Fellow Israelites, help! This is the man who's going all over the world spreading lies against us, our religion, and this place. He's even brought Greeks in here and defiled this holy place." (What had actually happened: they'd seen Paul and Trophimus, the Ephesian Greek, walking together in the city and just assumed Paul had also brought him into the Temple.)

Soon the whole city was in an uproar, with people streaming from everywhere to the Temple to join in. They seized Paul, dragged him outside, and locked the Temple gates so he couldn't get back in and claim sanctuary.

While they were trying to kill him, word reached the Roman commander: "Riot! The whole city's boiling over!" He acted fast. His soldiers and centurions rushed to the scene. The moment the mob saw the commander and his soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

The commander came up and arrested Paul. First he ordered him handcuffed, then asked who he was and what he'd done. All he got from the crowd was shouting — one yelling this, another that. It was impossible to make out a word in the mob frenzy, so the commander ordered Paul taken to the barracks. But when they reached the Temple steps, the mob got so violent the soldiers had to carry Paul. As they carried him off, the crowd trailed behind, chanting, "Kill him! Kill him!"

When they reached the barracks and were about to go inside, Paul said to the commander, "Can I say something to you?" He answered, "Oh, I didn't know you spoke Greek. I thought you were the Egyptian who started a riot here not long ago and then hid out in the desert with his four thousand rebels."
Paul said, "No, I'm a Jew, born in Tarsus — and I'm still a citizen of that important city. I have one simple request: let me speak to the crowd."
§ Paul Tells His Story
Standing on the barracks steps, Paul raised his arms. A hush fell over the crowd as Paul began to speak. He spoke in Hebrew.

title: Paul Tells His Story to the Angry Crowd
paragraphs: "My dear brothers and fathers, listen carefully to what I have to say before you make up your minds about me." When they heard him speaking in Hebrew, they grew even quieter. Nobody wanted to miss a single word.

He continued, "I'm a true Jew — born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but educated right here in Jerusalem under the strict eye of Rabbi Gamaliel, trained thoroughly in our religious traditions. And I've always been passionately on God's side, just like you are right now."

"I hunted down everyone connected with this 'Way' with everything I had, ready to kill for God. I rounded up men and women left and right and threw them in prison. You can ask the high priest or anyone on the council — they all knew me well. Then I headed off to our brothers in Damascus, carrying official letters authorizing me to track down the followers of Jesus there, arrest them, and bring them back to Jerusalem for sentencing."
"As I neared Damascus around noon, a blinding light blazed out of the sky and I hit the ground, dazed. I heard a voice: 'Saul, Saul, why are you trying to destroy me?'"
"'Who are you, Lord?' I asked. He answered, 'I am Jesus of Nazareth — the very One you're persecuting.' My companions saw the light, but they couldn't hear him speaking to me."

"Then I said, 'What do I do now, Master?' He said, 'Get up and go into Damascus. There you'll be told everything you've been assigned to do.' And so we went into Damascus — but nothing like the entrance I'd planned. I was blind as a bat, and my companions had to lead me in by the hand."

"That's when I met Ananias, a man with a spotless reputation for keeping our laws — the whole Jewish community in Damascus agrees on that. He came and put his arm around my shoulder. 'Look up,' he said. I looked up — and found myself staring right into his eyes. I could see again!"

"Then he said, 'The God of our ancestors has handpicked you to learn his plan. You've actually seen the Righteous One and heard him speak. You're going to be a key witness to everyone you meet about what you've seen and heard. So what are you waiting for? Get up, get baptized, wash your sins away, and get to know God personally.'"

"It happened just as Ananias said. After I was back in Jerusalem, praying one day in the Temple, deep in God's presence, I saw him — God's Righteous One — and heard him say to me, 'Hurry! Get out of here as fast as you can. None of the Jews here in Jerusalem are going to accept what you say about me.'"

"At first I argued back: 'Who has better credentials than me? They all know how obsessed I was with hunting down your believers — beating them in the synagogues and throwing them in jail. And when your witness Stephen was killed, I was right there, holding the murderers' coats and cheering them on. Now they see me completely changed. What better proof could there be?'"
"But he said, 'Stop arguing. Go. I'm sending you far away to the non-Jewish outsiders.'"
§ A Roman Citizen

The crowd had listened carefully up to this point, but now they exploded, shouting, "Kill him! He's scum! Get rid of him!" They shook their fists. They filled the air with curses. That's when the commander stepped in and ordered Paul taken into the barracks. By now the commander was completely fed up. He decided to interrogate Paul under torture to get to the bottom of this — to find out what he'd done to trigger such furious violence. As they stretched him out with leather straps, getting him ready for the whip, Paul said to the centurion standing there, "Is this legal — torturing a Roman citizen without a trial?"
When the centurion heard that, he went straight to the commander. "Do you know what you've done? This man is a Roman citizen!"
The commander came back and took charge. "Is what I hear true? You're a Roman citizen?" Paul said, "I certainly am."
The commander was impressed. "I paid a fortune for my citizenship. How much did yours cost?" "Nothing," said Paul. "It didn't cost me a thing. I was born free."
That ended the interrogation on the spot. And it scared the commander half to death — he'd put a Roman citizen in chains and nearly had him tortured!

The next day, determined to get to the root of the trouble and find out exactly what was behind the Jewish accusations, the commander released Paul and ordered a meeting of the chief priests and the whole council to see what they could make of it. Paul was brought in and took his place before them.

title: A Nephew's Tip-Off and a Midnight Rescue
paragraphs: § Before the High Council

Paul looked straight at the council members and said his piece: "Friends, I've lived with a clear conscience before God my whole life, right up to this very moment." That set off the high priest Ananias. He ordered his aides to slap Paul across the face. Paul fired back, "God is going to strike you down! What a hypocrite you are! You sit there judging me by the Law, then break the Law by ordering me slapped!"
The aides were shocked: "How dare you talk to God's high priest like that!"

Paul acted surprised. "How was I supposed to know he was the high priest? He sure doesn't act like one. You're right — Scripture does say, 'Don't speak evil of a ruler of your people.' Sorry about that."

Paul knew the council was split between Sadducees and Pharisees — and how much they despised each other — so he decided to use their rivalry: "Friends, I'm a die-hard Pharisee from a long line of Pharisees. I'm on trial here because of my Pharisee beliefs — the hope of the resurrection of the dead."

The second he said that, the council split down the middle, Pharisees and Sadducees going at each other in a heated shouting match. The Sadducees don't believe in resurrection, angels, or spirits — if they can't see it, they don't buy it. The Pharisees believe in all of it. So a massive, noisy brawl broke out. Then some of the Pharisee legal experts shouted the others down: "We don't find anything wrong with this man! What if a spirit spoke to him? Or an angel? What if we end up fighting against God?"

That threw gasoline on the fire. The fight flared up so violently the commander was afraid they'd tear Paul limb from limb. He ordered the soldiers to pull him out of there and escort him back to the safety of the barracks.
§ A Plot Against Paul
That night the Master came to Paul: "Don't be afraid. It's all going to work out. You've been a faithful witness for me here in Jerusalem — and now you're going to witness for me in Rome!"

The next day, the Jews hatched a plot against Paul. They took a solemn oath not to eat or drink until they'd killed him. More than forty of them bound themselves to this murder pact and went to the chief priests and elders. "We've sworn a solemn oath to eat nothing until we've killed Paul. But we need your help. Have the council ask the commander to bring Paul down tomorrow, as if you want to investigate the charges more carefully. We'll handle the rest. Before he gets anywhere near you, we'll kill him. Your hands stay clean."

But Paul's nephew — his sister's son — overheard them planning the ambush. He went straight to the barracks and told Paul. Paul called over one of the centurions and said, "Take this young man to the commander. He's got something important to tell him."
The centurion took him to the commander and said, "The prisoner Paul asked me to bring this young man to you — he has something urgent to report."
The commander took the young man by the arm and led him aside privately. "What is it? What do you need to tell me?"

Paul's nephew said, "The Jews have cooked up a plot against Paul. Tomorrow morning they're going to ask you to bring Paul to the council, claiming they want to investigate the charges against him more thoroughly. But it's a trap to get him out of your custody so they can kill him. Right now more than forty men are lying in ambush for him. They've all vowed not to eat or drink until they've killed him. Everything's set — they're just waiting for you to send him over."
The commander sent the nephew off with a warning: "Don't breathe a word of this to anyone."

The commander called two centurions. "Get two hundred soldiers ready to leave for Caesarea immediately. Add seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. I want them ready to march by nine o'clock tonight. And get a couple of horses for Paul and his gear. We're delivering this man safe and sound to Governor Felix."

Then he wrote this letter: From Claudius Lysias, to His Excellency Governor Felix: Greetings! I rescued this man from a Jewish mob. They'd grabbed him and were about to kill him when I found out he was a Roman citizen — so I sent in my soldiers. I wanted to know what he'd done wrong, so I brought him before their council. It turned out to be a vicious squabble over their religious differences — nothing even close to a crime. Then I learned they'd cooked up a plot to murder him. I decided the safest move was to get him out of here fast. So I'm sending him to you, and I've told his accusers to present their case before you.

The soldiers followed orders and took Paul that same night to safety in Antipatris. In the morning the foot soldiers returned to their barracks in Jerusalem, while the cavalry escorted Paul on to Caesarea. The horsemen rode into Caesarea and handed Paul and the letter over to the governor.

After reading the letter, the governor asked Paul which province he was from and was told "Cilicia." Then he said, "I'll hear your case when your accusers arrive." He ordered Paul locked up for now in King Herod's palace.

title: Paul on Trial
paragraphs: § Paul States His Defense

Within five days, the high priest Ananias arrived with a group of leaders and Tertullus, a trial lawyer. They laid out their case against Paul before the governor. When Paul was brought into court, Tertullus spoke for the prosecution: "Your Excellency Felix, we are deeply grateful at all times and in all places for your wise and gentle rule. We know full well that it's thanks to you — and you alone — that we enjoy this peace and benefit daily from your reforms. I won't wear you out with a long speech. I just ask your kindness in hearing me out. I'll keep it brief."

"We've caught this man again and again disturbing the peace, stirring up riots among Jews all over the world — the ringleader of a troublemaking sect called the Nazarenes. He's a genuine menace, I have to say. We caught him trying to defile our holy Temple and arrested him. You'll be able to confirm every one of these charges when you question him yourself."
The other Jews chimed in: "Hear, hear! That's right!"

The governor nodded for Paul to speak. Paul said, "I consider myself lucky to defend myself before you, Governor, knowing how fairly you've judged our nation all these years. I've only been back in the country twelve days — you can easily check those dates. I came specifically to worship in Jerusalem for Pentecost, and I've been minding my own business the entire time. Nobody can say they saw me arguing in the Temple or stirring up crowds in the streets. Not one of their charges can be backed up with evidence or witnesses."

"But I'll freely admit this: when it comes to the Way, which they trash as a dead end, I serve and worship the very same God our ancestors served and worshiped, and I embrace everything written in our Scriptures. And yes, I live in hopeful expectation that God will raise the dead — both the righteous and the wicked. If that's a crime, my accusers are just as guilty as I am."

"Believe me, I do my absolute best to keep a clear conscience before God and people in everything I do. I'd been out of the country for years and have only now returned. While I was away, I collected money for the poor and brought it with me, along with offerings for the Temple. It was while presenting those offerings that they found me quietly praying in the Temple. No crowd, no disturbance. It was some Jews from the Ephesus area who started all this trouble. And notice — they're not here today. They're cowards, too afraid to accuse me to your face."

"So ask these people here what crime they've actually caught me committing. Don't let them hide behind this smooth talker Tertullus. The only thing they have on me is that one line I shouted in the council: 'I'm on trial because I believe in the resurrection!' Does that sound like grounds for a criminal case to you?"

Felix stalled. He actually knew a lot more about the Way than he let on and could have settled the case right then. But unsure of his best political move, he played for time. "When Commander Lysias comes down, I'll decide your case." He ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody but to give him a fair amount of freedom and let his friends help him.

A few days later, Felix and his wife Drusilla — who was Jewish — sent for Paul and listened as he talked about a life of faith in Jesus Christ. As Paul kept pressing on right living before God and people, on moral self-discipline, and on the coming judgment, Felix started feeling uncomfortably close to home and cut him off. "That's enough for today. I'll call you back when it's convenient." At the same time, he was secretly hoping Paul would offer him a fat bribe. These conversations happened over and over.
Two years passed like this. Then Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. Still currying favor with the Jews and brushing justice aside, Felix left Paul locked up in prison.

title: Paul Appeals to Caesar
paragraphs: § An Appeal to Caesar

Three days after Festus arrived in Caesarea to start his job as governor, he went up to Jerusalem. The chief priests and top leaders revived their grudge against Paul. They asked Festus to do them a favor and have Paul brought to Jerusalem to answer their charges. A lie, of course — they'd revived their old plan to ambush and kill him on the way.

Festus replied that Paul's case belonged in Caesarea, and that he himself would be going back there shortly. "You're free," he said, "to travel back with me and bring whatever charges you think he deserves."

About eight or ten days later, Festus returned to Caesarea. The next morning he took his seat in the courtroom and had Paul brought in. The moment Paul walked in, the Jews who'd come down from Jerusalem swarmed him, throwing the wildest accusations at him — not one of which they could prove.
Then Paul took the stand and said simply, "I've done nothing wrong against the Jewish law, or the Temple, or Caesar. Period."
Festus, though, wanted to win favor with the Jews, so he said, "How would you like to go up to Jerusalem and let me try your case there?"

Paul answered, "Right now I'm standing before Caesar's court, where I have every right to stand — and I'm staying here. I've done nothing wrong to the Jews, and you know it as well as I do. If I've committed a crime and deserve to die, name the day. I can face that. But if there's nothing to their accusations — and you know there isn't — nobody can hand me over to them. We've wasted enough time here. I appeal to Caesar."
Festus conferred briefly with his advisors, then gave his verdict: "You've appealed to Caesar — to Caesar you will go!"

A few days later, King Agrippa and his wife Bernice visited Caesarea to welcome Festus to his new post. After several days, Festus brought up Paul's case with the king. "I've got a prisoner on my hands here, left behind by Felix. When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and Jewish leaders piled accusations on him and wanted me to sentence him to death. I told them that's not how we Romans do things. Just because someone's accused, we don't throw him to the wolves. We make sure the accused gets to face his accusers and defend himself against the charges. So when they came down here, I got right on the case. I took my seat in the courtroom and put the man on trial."

"The accusers came at him from every angle, but their charges turned out to be nothing but arguments about their religion and a dead man named Jesus, whom the prisoner claims is alive. Since I'm new here and don't fully grasp cases like this, I asked if he'd go to Jerusalem and stand trial there. Paul refused and demanded a hearing before His Majesty in our highest court. So I ordered him kept in custody until I could send him to Caesar in Rome."
Agrippa said, "I'd like to see this man and hear his story myself." "Good," said Festus. "We'll bring him in first thing tomorrow morning."

The next day, everyone who was anyone in Caesarea made their way to the audience hall, along with the top military officers. Agrippa and Bernice made a grand, sweeping entrance and took their seats. Then Festus ordered Paul brought in.

Festus said, "King Agrippa and distinguished guests, take a good look at this man. Crowds of Jews petitioned me — first in Jerusalem, then here — to get rid of him. They've been screaming for his execution. I looked into it and concluded he'd committed no crime. He asked for a trial before Caesar, and I agreed to send him to Rome. But what am I supposed to write to my lord Caesar? Every charge the Jews made was made up, and I've found nothing else."

"That's why I've brought him before all of you — and especially you, King Agrippa: so we can come up with some kind of charge that actually holds up. Because it seems ridiculous to me to send a prisoner all that way for trial without being able to say what he did wrong."

title: Paul's Defense Before Agrippa
paragraphs: § "I Couldn't Just Walk Away"

Agrippa spoke directly to Paul: "Go ahead — tell us your side." Paul took his stand and told his story. "I can't think of anyone, King Agrippa, I'd rather defend myself against these Jewish accusations before than you — you know Jewish customs and all our internal disputes so well."

"Since my youth, my whole life has been lived among my own people in Jerusalem. Practically every Jew in town who watched me grow up — and if they were brave enough they'd tell you to your face — knows I lived as a strict Pharisee, the most demanding branch of our religion. It's because I believed it and took it seriously — committing myself heart and soul to what God promised our ancestors, the very same hope the twelve tribes have clung to day and night all these centuries — it's because I've held on to this tested, proven hope that the Jews are dragging me into court. They should be the ones on trial here, not me! I honestly can't see why believing that God raises the dead is a crime."

"I'll admit I didn't always hold this view. For a while I thought it was my duty to fight this Jesus of Nazareth with everything I had. Armed with full authority from the chief priests, I threw these believers — I had no idea they were God's people! — into Jerusalem jails left and right, and whenever a vote came up, I voted to execute them. I raged through their synagogues, bullying them into cursing Jesus — a one-man wrecking crew obsessed with wiping these people out. Then I started in on towns outside Jerusalem."

"One day, on my way to Damascus — armed as always with papers from the chief priests authorizing my mission — right in the middle of the day, a blaze of light brighter than the sun poured out of the sky onto me and my companions. Oh, King, it was blinding! We fell flat on our faces. Then I heard a voice in Hebrew: 'Saul, Saul, why are you trying to destroy me? Why do you keep fighting against me?'"

"I said, 'Who are you, Master?' The voice answered, 'I am Jesus, the One you're hunting like an animal. But now, get up — I have a job for you. I've handpicked you to be my servant and witness to what happened today, and to what I'm going to show you."

"'I'm sending you to open the eyes of the outsiders, so they can see the difference between darkness and light and choose light — see the difference between Satan and God and choose God. I'm sending you to offer them forgiveness of sins and a place in the family, inviting them into the company of everyone who begins truly living by believing in me.'"

"What could I do, King Agrippa? I couldn't just walk away from a vision like that! I became an obedient believer on the spot. I started preaching this life-change — this radical turn to God and what it means in everyday life — right there in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and the surrounding countryside, and from there to the whole world."

"It's because of this 'whole world' part that the Jews grabbed me in the Temple that day and tried to kill me. They want to keep God to themselves. But God has stood by me, just as he promised, and here I am saying what I've been saying to anyone who'll listen, king or child. And everything I'm saying lines up completely with what the prophets and Moses said would happen: first, the Messiah had to die; second, raised from the dead, he would be the first rays of God's daylight shining on people far and near — the godless and the God-fearing alike."
That was too much for Festus. He burst out: "Paul, you're out of your mind! Too many books, too much staring into space! Snap out of it — come back to reality!"

But Paul held his ground. "With all due respect, Your Honor Festus, I'm not crazy. What I'm saying is true and sane. The king knows what I'm talking about — I'm sure none of this sounds crazy to him. He's known about it all for a long time. This wasn't done in some dark corner, you know. You believe the prophets, don't you, King Agrippa? Don't answer — I know you believe."
But Agrippa did answer: "Keep this up much longer and you'll talk me into becoming a Christian!"
Paul, chains and all, answered, "That's my prayer — sooner or later — that not only you but everyone here today would become what I am. Minus, of course, these chains!"

The king and the governor, along with Bernice and their advisors, got up and went into the next room to discuss what they'd heard. They quickly agreed Paul was innocent, saying, "There's nothing about this man that deserves prison, let alone death."
Agrippa told Festus, "He could be set free right now if he hadn't appealed to Caesar."

title: The Great Storm and the Shipwreck
paragraphs: § A Storm at Sea

As soon as the arrangements were complete for our voyage to Italy, Paul and several other prisoners were put under the charge of a centurion named Julius, from an elite regiment. We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was headed for Ephesus and ports west along the Asia coast. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, came with us.
The next day we docked at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly — he let him go ashore and enjoy the hospitality of his friends there.

Back out at sea, we sailed north along the sheltered side of Cyprus, northeast of the island, because strong westerly winds were against us, then westward along the coast to the port of Myra. There the centurion found an Egyptian grain ship bound for Italy and transferred us aboard. We hit rough weather and couldn't hold our course. After a long, hard struggle, we finally reached the southern coast of Crete and docked at Fair Havens — fitting name!

By now we'd lost a lot of time. The autumn sailing season was over, so from here through winter it would be stormy — too dangerous for sailing. Paul warned them: "I can see nothing but disaster ahead for the cargo and the ship — not to mention our lives — if we set sail now."

But Fair Havens wasn't a great harbor for spending the winter. Phoenix, a few miles farther along, was much better. The centurion ignored Paul's warning and let the ship's captain and owner talk him into trying for the next harbor.

When a gentle south wind started blowing, they weighed anchor, thinking it would be smooth sailing. But no sooner were they out at sea than a hurricane-force wind — the infamous northeaster — slammed into them. They lost all control of the ship. It was like a cork in the storm.

We ran under the shelter of a small island called Clauda and barely managed to secure the lifeboat and take in sail. Rocky shoals kept us from getting close to shore. We only avoided them by dropping sea anchors.

The next day, back out on the open sea and badly battered by the storm, we threw the cargo overboard. On the third day the crew lightened the ship further by tossing all the tackle and gear. For days we hadn't seen sun or stars. Wind and waves were pounding us mercilessly, and we lost all hope of being rescued.

With everyone's appetite for food — and for life — long gone, Paul stood up among us and said, "Friends, you really should have listened to me back in Crete. We could have avoided all this damage and loss. But no point dwelling on that now. From here on, things are looking up! I can promise you that not one of us will drown — though I can't say the same for the ship. The ship is doomed."

"Last night an angel of God stood beside me — the God I serve — and said, 'Don't be afraid, Paul. You still have to stand trial before Caesar — and God has graciously given you the lives of everyone sailing with you.' So take heart, friends! I believe God will do exactly what he told me. But we are going to run aground on some island."

On the fourteenth night, drifting somewhere in the Adriatic Sea, around midnight the sailors sensed land was near. They dropped a weighted line and measured about 120 feet deep; a little later, about 90 feet. Afraid we'd run aground on the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight.

Some of the sailors tried to abandon ship. They lowered the lifeboat, pretending they were going to drop more anchors from the bow. Paul saw right through it and told the centurion and the soldiers, "Unless these sailors stay with the ship, we're all going down." So the soldiers cut the lifeboat's ropes and let it drift away.

Just before dawn, Paul gathered everyone and suggested breakfast: "Today is the fourteenth day you've gone without food. None of you has felt like eating! But I'm urging you to eat something now. You'll need your strength for what's ahead. You're going to come through this without a scratch!"
He broke bread, thanked God, passed it around, and they all ate heartily — 276 of us in all! With the meal over and everyone full, they lightened the ship further by dumping the grain into the sea.

At daybreak, no one recognized the land — but then they spotted a bay with a sandy beach. They decided to try running the ship aground there. They cut the anchor ropes, untied the rudders, hoisted the foresail, and headed for the beach with the wind behind them. But they didn't make it. Still far from shore, they struck a sandbar, and the ship started breaking apart.

The soldiers decided to kill the prisoners so none could swim away and escape — but the centurion, determined to save Paul, stopped them. He ordered everyone who could swim to jump overboard first and head for shore, and the rest to grab planks or pieces of the ship. Everyone made it to land safely.

title: Snakebite on Malta
paragraphs: Once everyone was accounted for and we realized we'd all made it, we learned we were on the island of Malta. The locals went out of their way to be kind to us. It was rainy and cold, and we were soaked to the bone — but they built a huge bonfire and gathered us around it.

Paul pitched in to help. He'd gathered an armful of sticks, but when he laid it on the fire, a venomous snake — jolted awake by the heat — sank its fangs into his hand and hung on. Seeing the snake dangling from Paul's hand, the locals jumped to the conclusion that he was a murderer getting what he deserved. Paul just shook the snake off into the fire like it was nothing. They kept waiting for him to keel over dead — but when it became obvious he wasn't going to, they flipped to the opposite conclusion: he must be a god!

The leading man on that part of the island was Publius. He welcomed us into his home as his guests, dried us out, and hosted us in fine style for three days. Publius's father was sick at the time — down with a high fever and dysentery. Paul went into the old man's room, laid hands on him, prayed — and the man was healed. News of the healing spread fast, and soon every sick person on the island came and was healed.
§ Rome

We spent an amazing three months on Malta. They treated us like royalty, met all our needs, and stocked us up for the rest of the journey. When an Egyptian ship that had wintered in the harbor got ready to sail for Italy, we boarded. The ship's figurehead was the twin gods Castor and Pollux — "the Heavenly Twins."

We docked at Syracuse for three days, then sailed up the coast to Rhegium. Two days later, with a south wind behind us, we sailed into the Bay of Naples. We found Christian friends there and stayed with them for a week.

And then we reached Rome. Friends in Rome heard we were coming and came out to meet us. One group came as far as the Forum of Appius; another met us at the Three Taverns — emotional reunions, as you can imagine. Paul, overflowing with praise, led us in prayers of thanksgiving. When we actually entered Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier assigned to guard him.

Three days later, Paul invited the local Jewish leaders to meet at his house. He said, "Fellow Jews, the leaders in Jerusalem arrested me on trumped-up charges, and I ended up in Roman custody. I want you to know I did absolutely nothing against our laws or our customs. After the Romans investigated and found nothing to the charges, they wanted to let me go — but the Jews objected so fiercely that I was forced to appeal to Caesar. I didn't do it to accuse our people of anything or to get them in trouble with Rome — we've had more than enough of that kind of trouble over the years. I did it *for* Israel. I asked you here today to make it clear that I'm on Israel's side, not against her. I'm chained here because of hope, not doom."

They said, "Nobody wrote to warn us about you, and no one has shown up with anything bad to say about you. But we'd really like to hear more. The only thing we know about this Christian movement is that people everywhere seem to speak against it."

They set a date. When the day came, they returned to his house with quite a few friends. Paul talked to them all day long, from morning till evening — explaining everything about the kingdom of God and trying to persuade them about Jesus, pointing to what Moses and the prophets had written about him.

Some were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe a word. When the unbelievers got cranky and started arguing among themselves, Paul cut in: "I have just one more thing to say. The Holy Spirit knew exactly what he was talking about when he spoke to our ancestors through the prophet Isaiah: Go to this people and tell them: 'You will listen with your ears but never understand; you will look with your eyes but never see. These people are stubborn! They plug their ears so they don't have to listen; they shut their eyes so they don't have to look — so they won't have to face me and let me heal them.'"
"You've had your chance. The non-Jewish outsiders are next. And believe me — they're going to welcome it with open arms!"

Paul lived two whole years in his rented house. He welcomed everyone who came to see him. He boldly proclaimed everything about the kingdom of God. He taught all about Jesus Christ. His door was always open.
